Lastly, we found that the homogenization outcome for a specific almost periodic template is equivalent to a constant value that is the average of the two extreme material conductivities. This technique is particularly valuable for developing models that can analyze complex cancer images with varying accuracy. The success of this study suggests that FL-RL can be an effective solution for developing reliable and accurate models for cancer image analysis in real-world settings. Recently, RL has been applied to quadrupedal locomotion, but current methods face significant challenges due to the complex relationship between control inputs and movement. Most RL methods rely on controllers that directly utilize sensory data, but this approach is limited by the short lifespan of individual foot states. Our solution involves an innovative evolutionary generator creating trajectories for each foot to enhance learning stability and enable longer training lifespans. By leveraging these trajectories, each foot can be controlled through path following, which simplifies the task and increases learning efficiency. Our method achieves notable results, as the quadrupedal robot Amica successfully navigates diverse terrains at a steady pace of 0.5m/s, outperforming previous achievements by 50%. Moreover, our controller enables the robot to cross a 30cm-wide pit without human intervention. Our research indicates that combining evolutionary path planning with RL control is an effective strategy for tackling complex locomotion challenges. A key factor in understanding these objects is the feedback mechanism that prevents the black hole from exceeding the Eddington limit, but the origin of this feedback is still a topic of debate.  We investigated the origin of this feedback through a study of the dynamics of a low-luminosity active galactic nuclei using a 3D hydrodynamic simulation, assuming a steady accretion flow.  We found that a significant portion of the kinetic energy is concentrated in the turbulent movement of gas in the vicinity of the black hole, and this finding is consistent with recent observational results.  We also discovered that the movement pattern of the gas is similar to the characteristics observed in the central regions of the Milky Way.  As a result, we concluded that the kinetic energy associated with the movement of gas in the vicinity of the black hole could be a key factor in understanding the feedback mechanism. Closed-loop system performance can decline over time due to aging dynamics in systems such as wearable technology or systems affected by wear and tear. Replacing the original controller from scratch is inefficient because it overlooks the existing dynamics of the aging system. Furthermore, using traditional reinforcement learning to redesign the controller becomes labor-intensive and less effective due to the long training period, high sample requirements, and the inability to transfer knowledge across tasks. To address these challenges, we introduce a method to redesign a closed-loop system controller in a task-agnostic setting, enabling the systematic reduction of sample needs and enhancing the transfer of knowledge across tasks. We achieve this through a two-step process involving the inversion of the system dynamics using simulation-based methods and the optimization of the controller using a task-agnostic reinforcement learning framework. The efficacy of our approach was validated through simulations of a model-based wearable healthcare system. When compared to a reinforcement learning redesign using system dynamics, our method demonstrated improved performance, enhanced sample efficiency, and increased task across-fertilization capabilities. Specifically, we observed a 90% enhancement in sample efficiency, along with the transfer of knowledge across tasks in a 2-task set with similar dynamics without requiring re-training. Developing models capable of comprehending code is essential for various applications, including automated testing and debugging. While neural network models have excelled in code analysis, their reliance on extensive training data and specialized hardware render them impractical for widespread adoption. In contrast, the graph neural network model we introduce requires only minimal training and omits the need for explicit syntax knowledge. By representing code as a graph, our model captures essential features such as function definitions, variable scopes, and connections between variables, which it leverages to derive a unified function representation. When applied to various tasks, this model consistently outperforms prior methods, showcasing the efficacy of graph-based code representation and machine learning. In particular, our model achieves remarkable performance on program summarization, variable identification, and code summarization, surpassing human performance in certain evaluations. Furthermore, our model demonstrates remarkable cross-language versatility by adapting seamlessly to new languages following minimal training. In addition to outstanding empirical performance, our model boasts exceptional interpretability, facilitated by graph visualization and attention analysis that illuminates the role of each node in code analysis. In line with our goal of making code analysis more accessible, our model, codegraphs, is now freely available for download. This paper builds upon the Graphical Lasso, a statistical method that estimates Gaussian network structures in a Bayesian framework, offering a variational inference alternative to Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling. The underlying model is a sparsity-promoting Gaussian distribution influenced by the l1 penalty. We demonstrate that this model can be reinterpreted as an unconstrained optimization problem, solving which yields the variational Bayes solution directly. This method provides an efficient, scalable alternative to the original Bayesian approach, while maintaining equivalent results. Experimental evaluations confirm the accuracy of our approach. Furthermore, we show that this scheme can be extended to non-Gaussian models, such as the nonparametric model for multivariate data. Optimization problems that have multiple objectives are challenging to solve due to the difficulty of deriving a precise utility function that reflects expert preferences. Involving experts is costly, and their feedback is often too specific for generalization. As a result, it is difficult to obtain a utility function that is accurate but easy to compute. We propose a new method that learns to summarize complex multi-dimensional information into a single value, compatible with various utility function forms and applicable to any optimization problem. This capability is leveraged to improve the efficiency of multi-dimensional optimization. We tested our approach on a real-world problem, which demonstrated its effectiveness in both simplifying the optimization process and improving its outcome. Additionally, the derived summarization tool can be useful independently for extracting important information from complex data.

We've developed a new model for simulating the creation and dispersal of nitrogen in the interstellar medium. This model separates nitrogen production between massive star explosions and changing AGB star luminosity, using realistic estimates of how these processes occur. When compared to real-world observations, our model shows that secondary nitrogen levels are lower than primary levels, especially in massive star clusters. This discrepancy is due to the delayed contribution of nitrogen from dying AGB stars. This delay is caused by the time it takes for these stars to form and explode, which is longer in denser clusters. This effect is most noticeable in such environments. This models' results are consistent with observations of massive star clusters, including the Eagle Nebula and the Carina Nebula, as well as data from the SDSS survey for the globular helium-rich cluster NGC 2808. These findings indicate that delayed AGB star contributions significantly affect nitrogen abundance in the interstellar medium, leading to lower secondary to primary ratios than previously thought. This could have significant implications for understanding the early universe's chemical composition. This models' predictions also extend to other astrophysical phenomena, such as planetary nebulae and supernovae, suggesting that further research into these areas may provide additional insights into its validity. This study introduces the Graph Privacy Advisor, a pioneering image privacy evaluation tool. Unlike conventional methods that rely on explicit user input, GPA leverages a neural network to quantify image privacy based on visual features. Specifically, GPA analyzes an uploaded image and compares it with the original, identifying the intensity of modifications made. This comparison is achieved through a similarity assessment facilitated by a graph matching algorithm. GPA's framework consists of three components: the visual representation transformer, which translates images into a format suitable for comparison; the graph matcher, which evaluates the similarity of images; and the privacy predictor, which determines the privacy level based on this evaluation. GPA was tested on three datasets and outperformed existing methods while requiring fewer resources. Notably, GPA demonstrated a 99% accuracy in detecting heavily modified MacBooks in the MUPO dataset and showed a positive correlation with the degree of modifications made in the DeepFashion dataset. Furthermore, experiments revealed that GPA improved image forgery detection by 5% and performed comparably to human assessments in evaluating the privacy of medical images. Small solar eruptions known as nanoflares may hold the key to explaining the solar corona's high temperatures due to the rapid release of magnetic energy through processes such as reconnection. This phenomenon is being studied using observations of footpoint emissions in EUV light. However, these observations often indicate that the energy released in nanoflares is insufficient to account for the coronal heating. This study investigates the underwhelming energy emitted in a nanoflare by using high-resolution data from the High-resolution Coronal imager, a camera that observes the He II 304 angstrom emission line. On October 18, 2020, the instrument detected a small solar flare in this wavelength range, indicating an energy release of around 10^19 ergs within a very localized area. Observations of the emission line continued for several minutes, revealing complex self-absorption effects due to the presence of cooler plasma at the footpoints. By modeling these effects, the study was able to estimate the total energy released in the flare, confirming previous findings that the energy emitted is significantly less than the total released energy, with about 10^18 ergs being emitted when around 10^20 ergs are released. This suggests that the energy released in the flare may be being directed away from the observed area, towards the interconnecting magnetic loops, possibly in the form of fast plasma jets. This new understanding of the flare's behavior could have significant implications for the study of solar nanoflares and coronal heating in general. This research is part of a larger project to study the properties of solar nanoflares using data from the High-resolution Coronal imager, with further findings expected to be published in the future. breaking down the process into two primary phases:

policy-based techniques, like distillation, that facilitate control as a 
guiding principle; 
2. Leveraging the insights gained to address the refined challenges, which 
may require different solution approaches, such as continuous or tree-based 
methods, facilitated by the 'distilled' control policies. 
We apply this framework successfully to tough planning problems within 
continuous domains, achieving favorable results compared to existing 
state-of-the-art methods. 
Moreover, this strategy also finds application in a novel approach for 
accelerating policy-based reinforcement learning by utilizing a planner for 
initial exploration. 
Our proposed methodology is documented in a companion report, along with 
experimental comparisons that demonstrate its effectiveness.

In contemporary data-driven inquiry, meticulous and continuous recording of 
research progress within an electronic lab notebook is advocated for as a means 
of managing provisional knowledge through deductive reasoning. This process not 
only aids in the identification of key data points but also enables the tracing 
of how initial observations evolve into meaningful outcomes. As such, we propose 
an innovative, fully automated system designed to safeguard users' entries in 
their electronic lab notebooks by pinpointing and alerting them to potential 
red flags, such as suspicious activity, characteristic of unauthorized access 
or internal sabotage. This protection mechanism is an essential component of 
our unified software platform for seamless integration with electronic lab 
notebooks, providing users with enhanced security and promoting a more secure 
research environment from initial data collection through final publication. 
Additionally, our platform also includes a cutting-edge analytical tool capable 
of conducting in-depth analyses across entire notebook histories, thereby 
facilitating the detection of internal threats and the identification of 
emerging trends within ongoing research endeavors. This approach has been 
thoroughly tested on multiple notebooks spanning diverse scientific fields 
science, revealing significant security vulnerabilities in existing electronic 
notebook solutions. Ultimately, our innovative solution offers a comprehensive 
solution for safeguarding electronic notebooks through a combination of 
protection mechanisms and in-depth analytical capabilities. Further details can 
be found in our full research paper available on arXiv at arXiv:2208.06919. For 
technical details regarding our research, please refer to the accompanying 
repository located at https://github.com/NeuJR/ELN-Protection, where additional 
resources including a live demo are also available for examination. Additionally, 
a video summarizing our research can be accessed via https://youtu.be/8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q.

High-entropy alloys are gaining significant attention due to their exceptional mechanical properties, yet their computational modeling is hindered by the need for simplified models. Machine learning algorithms can effectively address this gap, enabling the efficient learning of alloy properties from elemental characteristics. This review covers the latest developments in machine learning research on high-entropy alloys, focusing on theoretical and experimental advancements. It discusses how machine learning techniques are utilized to predictively modeling high-entropy alloy behavior, including their analysis of strengths and weaknesses in existing work. Furthermore, this review explores potential future research directions for further improving high-entropy alloys through machine learning-based design. Overall, machine learning is transforming the development of high-entropy alloys, enabling rapid identification of optimal compositions with improved mechanical properties. This includes accelerated exploration of vast composition spaces, facilitated by the prediction of mechanical properties from elemental and atomic structures. This review is organized into four sections, commencing with an overview of high-entropy alloys, followed by an examination of machine learning-based design, an evaluation of the current state of research, and finally suggesting promising research directions for future investigation. This comprehensive review aims to bridge the gaps between materials science, computer science, and data science to guide future research in the computational design of high-entropy alloys. This includes discussing the feasibility of applying artificial intelligence in the development of high-entropy alloys, building on the significant progress already made in this field. This includes developing efficient algorithms for global optimization in composition space and exploring the potential of generative adversarial networks to create new, high-performing compositions. This includes discussing the challenges and limitations of current research, such as the need for more extensive and diverse datasets, improved feature engineering, and the development of transparent and interpretable models. This includes evaluating the effectiveness of different machine learning techniques, such as regression, classification, clustering, dimensionality reduction, and generative models, in predicting high-entropy alloy behavior. This includes highlighting promising research directions, such as the integration of machine learning with other computational methods, such as first-principles calculations and meta-modeling, as well as the potential of new paradigms, such as knowledge graph learning, to improve the computational design of high-entropy alloys. This includes discussing the potential impact of machine learning on the development of high-entropy alloys, such as enabling the discovery of new compositions with improved mechanical properties, and reducing the need for experimental trials through predictive modeling. This includes evaluating the current state of research, such as the recent success of deep learning in predicting high-entropy alloy behavior, and identifying future research directions

Machine learning discovers hidden patterns in data by assuming certain variables are hidden from view. Developing effective methods for finding these latent variables is a pressing concern, and a promising approach involves treating them as complex variables with intricate internal structures. However, this goal is hindered by a long-standing theoretical limitation. We address this issue by proposing a novel method for estimating complex latent variables by assuming their internal structures are similar to those of observable variables. We evaluate this approach through experiments on simulated data and find it performs well. Moreover, we apply it to real-world data from a simple artificial world and find it accurately reconstructs the underlying structure. Finally, we discuss potential future directions for research. The method we developed is available online at https://github.com/alexwhartman/complex_state_estimation. We also created a basic simulator for exploring complex latent variable models at https://github.com/alexwhartman/latent_variable_simulator. Both of these tools are open-source and can be used by other researchers to validate our results or test new ideas. We hope these resources facilitate collaboration and encourage further innovation on the topic of latent variable learning. We also collected some additional results on how changing the design of latent variables affects learning in the appendix. We conducted a thorough investigation into the topic and found that well-designed latent variables can facilitate learning, while poorly designed ones can make it more difficult. We discovered that variables with too many internal states can be particularly challenging to learn and often result in models that are difficult to optimize. We also found that variables with too few internal states can make learning dependent on the order of the data. We did not find any benefits to using variables with circular dependencies or those with dependencies that do not affect their behavior. We did find however that variables with transitive dependencies - such as a car being made of parts - are well-suited for learning and can facilitate discovery of the underlying structure. We hope these findings are useful to other researchers and can inform the design of more effective latent variables for more complex artificial worlds. The measure of a vector-valued function's nonlinearity is essentially its deviation from affine functions. Researchers have recently identified upper limits for this nonlinearity; however, these limits have yet to be fully utilized. This study provides an explanation for this underutilization by demonstrating that any nonlinearity limit ultimately stems from previous, related findings. In addition, the concept of Sidon sets is crucial in this context, and this paper offers an enhanced understanding of these sets, including newly identified characteristics. Ultimately, the paper concludes by outlining avenues for further research. Notably, the paper introduces a concept known as near-Sidon sets, which are essentially sets with weakened Sidon conditions, and proves that achieving a nearly perfect saturation of this condition is feasible. This near-Sidon construction is derived from an earlier work by Li and Tu, which utilized a complex procedure involving the interlacing of two linear functions. In this study, a simplified alternative is presented, using a single linear function instead, and this new approach holds promise for potentially improving existing Sidon set upper limits. In support of this potential, the study provides examples of nearly perfect saturation of Sidon sets for vector-valued functions with a duality of 8, which surpasses previous records. This research also provides a new general upper bound for vector-valued functions' nonlinearity, which is essentially the total number of possible function outputs, minus the number that can be achieved through affine functions. In cases where the output space is small compared to its possible values, this nonlinearity is essentially zero. In other scenarios, this nonlinearity is at least half of the total possible values. Binary matrix datasets are widespread in research and structuring them by introducing zeros according to a underlying network is beneficial for identifying important factors. A popular method involves sampling a dense binary matrix from an exponential distribution conditioned on a pre-defined network-based permutation. Current sampling algorithms rely on Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques, utilizing algorithms like Gibbs or Metropolis-Hastings that suffer from slow convergence and poor mixing. Alternatively,'structural' algorithms are proposed which directly utilize the permutation to re-arrange matrix entries, but their effectiveness is limited by the matrix's sparsity level. In response, a new algorithm is developed that efficiently samples a dense binary matrix based on its permutation, demonstrated through empirical analysis showing superior performance in various fields when compared to traditional methods. The method, along with its implementation, can be accessed through the R package 'StructAlgo'.

We draw comparisons to an analogous model, consisting of real-valued components, allowing us to comprehend the effects of quantization. Our experiments demonstrate that quantized neural networks not only perform competitively with traditional models but also exhibit improved generalization capability, along with increased resistance to data corruption and adversarial attacks. A comprehensive analysis of the underlying mechanisms of quantization is also provided. Ultimately, the approach presented here serves as a trainable and versatile tool for designing efficient neural network models, capable of achieving a harmonious balance between performance and computational efficiency. Quantum systems possessing geometric duals exhibit a more restrictive set of entropy inequalities than general quantum systems do. Specifically, the set of achievable entropies for any subregion of the boundary is fully determined by its size in the bulk, as defined by the entropic HEC (Holographic Entropy Cone) theorem. In this paper, we derive a dual characterization of the NEC (Non-degenerate Entropy Cone), a more comprehensive set of entropy inequalities applicable to quantum systems, with the understanding that the NEC's constraints become activated only once the HEC's constraints are fully satisfied. Our characterization of the NEC involves two key components: a non-degenerate quantum channel linking the ambient space to a smaller one and an entropic quantity associated with the ambient space that exceeds its subregion entropies by at least their sum. Our findings imply that any boundary subregion with a HEC-compliant entropy profile can be coupled with a suitable bulk entropic structure, enabling the derivation of a corresponding boundary entropy profile that adheres to the stricter NEC standards, thereby effectively "upgrading" the HEC to NEC. Moreover, our results reveal that NEC-compliant systems are inherently capable of simulating any quantum system with a HEC-compliant entropy profile in its local ambient space, with the exception of those that would violate the HEC in doing so. Finally, our work shows that NEC-compliant systems can be constructed through the repeated application of resource theories within a fixed ambient space, with each iteration producing a non-degenerate quantum channel that is compatible with the previously generated resources, thereby providing a resource-theoretic foundation for the HEC-to-NEC "upgrades" discussed above. Our findings are further reinforced by concrete examples, with the specific case of random states serving as a particularly illuminating illustration of these concepts. Ultimately, our work offers a novel framework for understanding both the HEC and NEC inequalities as well-established milestones along a broader spectrum of entropy inequalities, with the NEC representing the most comprehensive set of entropy inequalities attainable through the repeated application of resource theories within a fixed ambient space. This perspective provides a unified understanding of both the HEC and NEC, clarifying their interrelationship and offering a concrete pathway for achieving the stricter NEC standards, with the potential to apply these findings to more efficiently construct bulk entropies satisfying the HEC. We examine a broad category of lattice models capable of exhibiting a non-equilibrium steady state through the application of constant external fields. A system where the stationary probability distribution follows a multi-component conformal field theory $T\!T_{\mathpzc{m}}(z,\bar{z})$ is chosen for in-depth analysis. By utilizing a duality transformation, we derive a precise expression for the crossing multiplier associated with the primary operator of this theory, with the result showing it is equal to the character of the operator's conformal family, calculated using the characters of the Virasoro algebra. Specifically, for the free fermion model ($T\!\mathpzc{m}^{(1)}(z,\bar{z})$), the character in question is given by the $\mathpzc{m}=1$ instance of a particular function, while for the hard-core loop model ($T\!\mathpzc{m}^{(2)}(z,\bar{z})$), the same character results from the product of two distinct functions. These findings align with existing data on conformal field theories. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the stationary probability distribution of the coupled classical-quantum lattice system follows a semi-conformal field theory, with the result showing the crossing multiplier associated with its primary operator is equal to the product of two distinct functions, each belonging to the characters of the Virasoro algebra. These results are verified through exact calculations and further validated by comparing them with data obtained from the coupled classical-quantum lattice system. The present work provides a significant advancement towards the goal of linking non-equilibrium steady state lattice models to conformal field theories. Moreover, it contributes novel insights into the relationship between crossing multipliers and the characters of conformal field theories, with the added benefit of revealing novel identities in the context of the Virasoro algebra. Lastly, it offers a novel approach to calculating the central charge of a given lattice model capable of reaching a non-equilibrium steady state through the application of constant external fields. This method can be employed even in scenarios where the free fermion algebra is not applicable, with the result showing the central charge is a weighted average of the characters of the algebra, with the weights determined by a set of crossing multipliers. We've developed mathematically rigorous definitions and properties for the concept of a well-behaved coadded image, applicable to both ground-based and space-based astronomy observations. Our focus is on capturing the essence of noise reduction in coadded images, yet this approach differs from conventional methods like median or mean coadds, even if they employ identical weights. Through rigorous mathematical analysis, we identify the criteria for linear coadds to maintain a well-defined point-spread function and examine the implications for nonlinear coadds. A detailed examination of common noise models highlights the challenges of recovering the original signal from nonlinear coadds. As a practical application, we demonstrate that linear coadds with uniform weights consistently yield the most favorable outcomes in terms of noise reduction and image resolution. Our research provides a solid foundation for the coadding technique, shedding light on the trade-offs between noise reduction, image resolution, and the shape of the point-spread function. Ultimately, this understanding positions coadds as an optimal approach for achieving high signal-to-noise ratios while preserving the native point-spread function. A comprehensive Python package, called pycoadd, is also introduced to facilitate the efficient computation of nonlinear coadds, specifically the median and weighted mean coadds. This package is actively used in the LSST-WFIRST project and is available on GitHub for public use. Furthermore, our research has also led to the development of a comprehensive documentation, including detailed case studies and a suite of tests to ensure pycoadd's reliability and scalability for handling large datasets. A separate GitHub repository contains this documentation, along with additional resources and code snippets to aid in the practical application of our research findings. Finally, as a testament to the practical utility of our research, we highlight its relevance to ongoing and future astronomical projects, including the LSST-WFIRST, the Roman, the Vera C. Miller and Sheffield discovered an equivalence between a Gaussian free field and the Dyson model's underlying stochastic process. Building upon their work, this note establishes an equivalence between another key model in probability theory, specifically the log-Gaussian shearfield, and a corresponding shearfield derived from the Dyson model. The chosen method of proof also leads to additional observations and a lesser-known yet important concept in the field of probability theory being linked to the Yang-Mills equation. The notes conclude with a broader discussion regarding the potential for such connections to occur between the domains of probability theory and differential equations. 

A significant amount of credit for the ideas presented within goes to Miller and Sheffield, while the Yang-Mills equation's connection is attributed to the work of Berman, Schubert, and Zygmun, in addition to Berman's published work. The field of probability theory is constantly evolving, and it is anticipated that further research will yield novel findings.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm. Our analysis extends earlier work by the authors in the two-dimensional setting to multi-dimensional space, and these estimates are comparable to those derived for the heat equations. These results are based on a novel approach that combines energy-based methods and the Fourier decomposition lemma to control the vorticity's maximum norm. This control, in turn, allows us to derive sharp maximum norm estimates for the velocity and, subsequently, the pressure. These estimates are further utilized to establish a Poincaré inequality for the Navier-Stokes equations' solutions, which are also shown to be smooth when the initial conditions are smooth. Finally, we demonstrate that our results can be extended to address the Cauchy problem for the Stokes equations and obtain analytical bounds for the inverse of the Stokes operator when applied to any divergence-free vector field. Our analysis is largely self-contained and relies only on fundamental mathematical principles, making it accessible to a broad audience interested in partial differential equations. These findings are expected to be useful in the study of the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations, particularly in analyzing the regularity of solutions to the hyperbolic Navier-Stokes equations and the critical case of the triple-point problem. Moreover, these results can be applied to establish the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem for the quasigeostrophic equations in multi-dimensional space. Additionally, our analysis is closely related to the study of the regularity of the solutions to the 3D Euler equations, particularly in analyzing the critical case of the triple-point problem. Furthermore, our results can be used to establish the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem for the quasigeostrophic equations in multi-dimensional space. Finally, our analysis is expected to be useful in the study of various problems related to the Navier-Stokes equations, such as the regularity of the solutions to the hyperbolic Navier-Stokes equations and the critical case of the triple-point problem. The verification problem for quantum computation is crucial because it enables clients to confirm that a quantum cloud service has correctly executed their submitted quantum states despite the potential for Moore's law slowdown in the quantum service's advantage over the client. Currently, the fastest classical verification of quantum computation protocol achieves a quadratic time complexity but requires exponentially large classical storage, limiting its application. We present an improved protocol that achieves a near-linear time complexity of O(polylog(k)) while reducing classical storage to poly(k) space. Additionally, we present an alternative protocol with a slightly higher time complexity of O(k^(l+1)} that requires significantly less storage, ultimately making it more efficient for large-scale computations. Notably, we prove that the near-linear time complexity is the best achievable given our current technical understanding, restricted only by the computational complexity barrier. Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically mimics the complex morphology of living cells, essential for training segmentation models and creating computational models of cell division, but accurately representing these shapes requires expertise due to their intricate nature. Current methods of representing cellular morphology often fail because voxel-based representations neglect spatial relationships and polygon meshes struggle to capture smooth shapes common in cells. Our approach involves representing cellular morphology as level sets of signed distance functions, which offer advantages in precision, flexibility, and ease of use. This method enables efficient sampling within these levels, allowing for the automatic addition of detailed features to coarse shapes, thus simplifying the creation of complex cell shapes. Additionally, our approach includes tools for editing shapes, propagating patterns, adapting existing shapes, and deforming them through the use of user-friendly interfaces, thus facilitating the easy creation of a wide variety of cell shapes. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of our approach in training a segmentation model and creating a computational model of cell division. Our software and generated cell shapes are available online.

Research on spatial perception and navigation has historically been rooted in Cartesian coordinates, but recent breakthroughs in neural networks have opened the door to exploring manifold-based alternatives that better align with animal cognition. Despite the plethora of neural network architectures, a unifying framework for spatial perception remains elusive, and it is unclear which one is most effective. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted an in-depth empirical investigation of popular spatial perception models, revealing that they often rely on implicit assumptions about the structure of environmental manifolds, which are unlikely to hold true in many scenarios. We therefore propose a new framework that combines a minimal set of explicit assumptions with a flexible manifold representation, striking a balance between simplicity and versatility. Empirically, our approach outperforms existing models on a range of challenging tasks involving noisy or distorted spatial inputs, as well as complex robotic navigation challenges inspired by animal cognition research. Notably, our method allows for the estimation of spatial coordinates without relying on a global coordinate system by leveraging local connectivity constraints, which can be implemented efficiently using recurrent networks. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a real-world robotic navigation task, achieving impressive results even with noisy sensor inputs. Our research provides a foundational understanding of spatial perception, enabling the creation of a versatile model that can be adapted to a wide range of spatial tasks. Moreover, our approach can be applied to various tasks beyond spatial perception, such as image recognition and language processing, as evidenced by our extensive experiments. Finally, our work highlights the importance of carefully selecting task-dependent assumptions when designing neural network architectures. All code is publicly available at https://github.com/krishanrana/SpatialPerception. Krishan Rana contributed equally to this work.

The primary goal of this research is to gain a deeper understanding of the theoretical foundations underlying the approximation of smooth functions using Gaussian analytic function zero sets, a challenge due to their highly irregular structure.
Despite this complexity, our study reveals that the approximation of certain functions within specific norm metrics on the zero set can be precisely calculated.
Specifically, we have derived exact formulas for interpolating polynomials on the zero set of Gaussian analytic functions in both $L^p$ norms for even $p$ values and also in the sup norm.
Furthermore, these formulas have a surprising connection to the Asymptotic Gaussian Process, an idealized generalization of Gaussian processes with controllable correlation functions.
Our findings can be extended to include functions beyond just polynomials, such as those with finite band width, a concept closely related to the Approximation Theory of Conformal Maps.
Additionally, we have discovered exact estimates for approximating smooth functions using Taylor series up to a certain degree on the zero set, a result that can be applied even when the function itself is not analytic.
Our analysis is supported by both numerical computations and relevant foundational theorems. Ultimately, this research provides a valuable connection between the complex structure of Gaussian analytic function zero sets and the powerful tools of Approximation Theory. Research indicates that there are two distinct types of El Ni\~no, East Pacific and Central Pacific, which have differing impacts on global seasonal precipitation patterns. To better understand these variations, scientists developed a new tool based on an ensemble of seasonal forecast models. By analyzing the performance of 15 models, they created a high-confidence forecast map for each season from April to November. When put through a rigorous testing process, these maps consistently showed that East Pacific and Central Pacific events tend to occur independently, contradicting the initial hypothesis that they were simply different manifestations of the same phenomenon. Furthermore, statistical models indicated that the probability of an East Pacific event is increased by anomalies in the equatorial Pacific, whereas central Pacific events are more likely when the equatorial Pacific shows the opposite signs. In contrast, the models suggested that the probability of a Central Pacific event is actually decreased by negative anomalies in the South Pacific, a phenomenon that has yet to be fully explained by existing climate theories. To further validate their findings, researchers conducted a comprehensive examination of the underlying physical processes governing these regional climate interactions. The formation history of massive black holes in galaxies is still a topic of significant debate. A theory suggests that massive black holes emerge in large, high-density regions known as globular clusters, although another scenario proposes that they originate from the merger of supermassive black holes within galaxies. To differentiate between these theories, researchers are examining the connection between the formation of these clusters and the appearance of peculiar star formations, specifically the presence of blue, metal-poor stars. By analyzing the metal content of individual stars in the Leo I dwarf galaxy using high-resolution spectroscopy, scientists discovered a notable separation between the galaxy's inner and outer regions. This distinction revealed two distinct populations of stars, characterized by their relatively low metal content and distinct ages. The outer region contains older, metal-poor stars, while the inner region holds younger, more metal-rich stars. This pattern suggests that Leo I underwent significant internal movement in the distant past, causing the galaxy's formation history to be obscured. The discovery in Leo I supports the idea that massive black holes emerge within dense star clusters, as the galaxy's central black hole is likely to have been created during this tumultuous event. The presence of a massive black hole in a galaxy like Leo I may be indicated by the presence of peculiar star formations, specifically the presence of He II emission. Future observations with the James Webb Space Telescope could potentially detect these star formations in numerous galaxies within the local universe. If detected, this could provide conclusive evidence for the massive black hole formation pathway in dwarf galaxies. Furthermore, the analysis of Leo I reveals that massive black holes are likely to be found in a significant portion of galaxies with a mass less than 10^6 solar masses. This finding has significant implications for the study of supermassive black hole growth in the early universe. The research team plans to further investigate this phenomenon by conducting a thorough study of the galaxy's central star cluster. This study is expected to shed more light on the early universe environment surrounding massive black holes. The research is supported by a grant from the National Science Foundation. In systems with electronic flat bands, quantum properties such as superconductivity, magnetism, and topological orders are frequently encountered. Due to geometric constraints, these flat bands are often found within structures like triangular, honeycomb, and kagome lattices. This review focuses on the concept of flat bands within kagome lattice frameworks, which occur naturally in small clusters or through careful engineering of moir\'e patterns with twisted bilayer materials. The theoretical models for these flat band kagome systems are examined, along with their predicted properties and potential outcomes when exposed to correlation effects. The recent detection of unusual flat band behavior in artificial kagome lattice constructs and natural diamond lattices is also discussed, along with prospects for future research into exotic properties in inherently two-dimensional kagome systems. Furthermore, the review explores potential future developments in emerging technologies, including topological orders and high-temperature superconductivity. Ultimately, the review concludes by highlighting the crucial importance of interdisciplinary research combining experimental measurements and theoretical analysis to fully comprehend the intricate behaviors of electronic flat band systems.

Previous studies have demonstrated that SNPs linked to specific traits exhibit a higher frequency of regulatory elements near their associated genes, particularly if these elements are located in close proximity to the genes themselves. A similar phenomenon has been observed in the case of DNase-I hypersensitive sites, which are indicative of active enhancer elements within cell nuclei. In this study, we sought to expand upon this discovery by examining the relationship between SNPs associated with particular traits and active enhancer elements across the entire human genome. Our research revealed a significant association between SNPs linked to specific traits and active enhancer elements located far away from their associated genes. This association was found to be more pronounced when the associated genes exhibited low levels of expression. To each multiplicative linear logic proof structure, we relate an ideal that encapsulates its logical meaning through polynomial equations. We demonstrate how cut-elimination in multiplicative proof nets parallels specific applications of the Buchberger algorithm, a method used for computing Gröbner bases in elimination theory. This connection reveals a unified reason behind the success of these algorithms. Furthermore, this framework enables examination of the complexity of solving multiplication-free logic problems, which we find to be NP-complete. Lastly, we explore how this framework can be extended to cover shared resources in multiplicative logic, achieving this extension at the cost of only allowing constructive rules.

THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystal lattices, leading to a considerable vibration of identifying ions. During this THz field, ions move in a circular motion, causing inertial effects that influence electrons' behavior. In our research, we demonstrate how to incorporate these inertial effects into computational models within a framework grounded in density functional theory. By incorporating the effects of ions' circular motion, new physical phenomena can be explored, such as the emergence of a Hall effect in the behavior of valence electrons. Our findings have the potential to expand the scope of theoretical and experimental investigations in condensed matter science. In particular, this research may facilitate the development of innovative materials exhibiting anomalous transport properties. In order to incorporate the effects of ions' circular motion, we derived mathematical expressions for the velocity and position gradients of ions, which we subsequently incorporated into existing approximations for the density functional. Notably, this incorporation does not introduce significant computational overhead. To validate our approach, we performed thorough tests on model systems, including hydrogen and helium, to verify its accuracy. These tests revealed that the incorporation of ions' circular motion has a negligible impact on previously established results. In contrast, the incorporation of inertial effects using a time-dependent density functional theory was found to be essential for accurate calculations in the presence of strong THz fields. In such scenarios, the incorporation of inertial effects could potentially reveal novel physical phenomena. Ultimately, our research may lead to innovative material discoveries, paving the way for groundbreaking applications in condensed matter science. proprietary nature of some data sources, processing is performed on local Linux

embedding computation on top of the Fog Orchestration and Governance framework.

usage, with the Fog platform outperforming other alternatives in time-series

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework illustrates the challenges in safeguarding dependent data and provides a strategic approach to maintaining sensitive location data privacy within urban areas. Our method efficiently suppresses the disclosure of sensitive information while maintaining the retention of important spatial characteristics for a given location. This is achieved using real-world data from the New York City taxi industry, where we show that our method surpasses existing techniques in maintaining both privacy and performance. Our source code is available at https://github.com/CompLogSociety/RDGP.

Building on previous work, we further develop directed graph analogues of the Ricci curvature and the Yang-Mills equation. By establishing a connection between these concepts, we demonstrate the existence of the Yang-Mills equation in the presence of Ricci curvature. Furthermore, we derive novel gradient estimates and prove the convergence of the Yang-Mills equation in the presence of directed graph Ricci curvature. Additionally, we present an application of our findings to the convergence of the Yang-Mills equation on general directed graphs. Lastly, we outline potential future research directions.

Recent advancements in neural machine translation for code-mixed languages like Spanish-English and Hindi-English have sparked interest, yet developing suitable word embeddings for these languages is a significant obstacle due to the limited availability of data.
Our research introduces SMEE, a novel word embedding model that effectively represents words from code-mixed texts by incorporating dual language information.
Through thorough evaluation on multiple fronts, we demonstrate that SMEE outperforms existing alternatives by achieving superior performance in downstream tasks, surpassing the performance of conventional neural machine translation models that rely on standard word embeddings. Furthermore, we showcase SMEE's ability to mitigate the challenges of low-resource learning, such as extreme data scarcity. Ultimately, our results indicate that SMEE provides a superior option for building word embeddings in code-mixed settings.

Utilizing a combination of density functional theory and the Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative technique, we investigated how the critical temperature of hydrogen sulfide varies with pressure. Our calculations indicated that the critical temperature of H3S increases rapidly with pressure, reaching nearly 200 K by 150 GPa. This enhancement is closely related to the pressure-dependent density of states at the Fermi level, which can be accurately predicted through functional derivatives. Additionally, we found that using a natural orbitals basis set significantly improves the convergence of our calculations in comparison to plane wave methods. At high pressures, the asymptotic behavior of the critical temperature is determined by the innermost electrons, thereby indicating a convergent trend. Furthermore, the shear modulus of H3S was calculated and our results show that it exhibits an unusual pressure-dependent behavior, initially decreasing before increasing at high pressures. Our findings are in good agreement with experimental data and recent ab initio predictions. Overall, the functional derivative technique proves to be an efficient tool for performing a wide range of high-pressure calculations. This method can be applied to a variety of materials, including those with complex crystal structures and extensive unit cells. Moreover, the use of functional derivatives enables the computation of second and third derivatives of mechanical and thermodynamic properties, thereby enabling precise simulations of high-pressure experiments. As a demonstration of its utility, we calculated the third derivative of the bulk modulus and predicted that it is nonzero. Furthermore, we evaluated the P-V-T behavior of H3S and determined that the phase transition from a tetragonal to an orthorhombic structure occurs at pressures above 140 GPa at 300 K. Our results are in good agreement with experimental data and provide a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of hydrogen sulfide under high pressure. This study also highlights the potential applications of superhydrides in the production of sustainable hydrogen energy. Based on our calculations, we propose that H3S and Li-aluminum hydride exhibit similar electronic properties, characterized by a small gap between the bonding and antibonding states. This unique property enables these materials to store a large amount of energy in chemical bonds, thereby making them promising candidates for the efficient production of hydrogen through chemical reactions. This research has significant implications for the development of innovative hydrogen energy technologies, thereby making it an important area of study in materials science. Although many studies have demonstrated correlation tools, few have effectively employed them to establish causal relationships. Our research introduces a novel method that enables the direct identification of causal relationships among a set of linked genetic variations and their corresponding physical outcomes within a cell. This is achieved through an optimization process constrained by data from individuals with genetic disorders and knowledge about the underlying cellular processes. Using this method, we have successfully simulated the discovery of a previously unknown causal relationship in a complex biological system. Furthermore, we have collaborated with researchers to apply our method to data from two real-world studies, one focused on a rare genetic disorder and the other on the link between a specific genetic variation and an increased risk of prostate cancer. This research focuses on resolving a specific problem in bipedal robot navigation. Due to limitations in finding suitable walking patterns that are both realistic and efficient from an energetic standpoint, robots often rely on pre-programmed gait patterns that are difficult to optimize. To address this challenge, a novel approach is presented for discovering a thrust profile through optimization. The proposed method produces a thrust profile as an integral output, eliminating the need for separate controller design. Key advantages of this approach include reduced computational demands, simplified design, and reduced thrust variability. To test its efficacy, a 10DOF bipedal robot was used to validate the proposed thrust profile algorithm in experimental trials. Results show that this algorithm enables the discovery of thruster input profiles with lower energetic requirements, allowing the robot to walk efficiently. Compared to traditional methods, the discovered gait patterns exhibited reduced energy consumption and improved stability. Specifically, energy consumption was decreased by approximately 20% and foot trajectory variability was limited to under 5 degrees. Successful application of this approach was confirmed through successful walking trials on various terrain types, including flat surfaces, inclined planes, and uneven ground. The associated time and space complexities of the proposed algorithm were found to be significantly lower than those of alternative optimization methods. Specifically, the discovered thruster input profiles exhibited a complexity of O(N logN), in contrast to O(N^2) for alternative methods. The issue of scheduling a robot's tasks efficiently is a long-studied problem,
but the conventional solutions either require predictive knowledge of tasks or
execute a separate planning process for each task, which is impractical for real-
time use cases. To address this, we developed a task scheduling method that
simultaneously balances processing a new task request with optimizing the queue
of pending tasks. This is achieved through a graph-based representation of tasks,
their solutions, and execution times, which are collectively referred to as task
descriptions. By efficiently reusing computational results from previous tasks,
we improved processing speeds significantly, allowing us to perform complex tasks
within 1ms and plan their execution. This resulted in a performance boost of 57x
and enabled online scheduling capabilities with no noticeable delay. Moreover, we
introduced a metric to evaluate the quality of a scheduling solution and used it
to assess our method's effectiveness in real-time applications by comparing it to
other state-of-the-art approaches. Experiment outcomes showed a 57x improvement in
scheduling time, allowing for timely execution of motions without noticeable delay.

The success of wireless data transmission is heavily reliant on the principles of diversity and dimensionality reduction. However, these principles are compromised when interference from other transmissions is considered, leading to the phenomenon of representational collapse, where the number of unique signal states is limited, regardless of the channel complexity. This research investigates the representational collapse in indoor wireless communications and its consequences. A mathematical model is developed to show that the number of unique signal states is directly proportional to the product of the correlation among interfering transmissions and the channel variability of the intended reception. This model reveals that the local delay, which includes both the processing time at the transmitter and the channel encoding rate, at least doubles as the correlation among interfering transmissions increases, assuming a given error probability. Furthermore, both the local delay and the error probability exhibit similar trends as the correlation changes. To mitigate the effects of representational collapse, a novel coding technique is proposed, which dynamically adjusts the modulation order based on the correlation among interfering transmissions. This approach is shown to outperform traditional methods, resulting in a significant decrease in delay while maintaining an acceptable error rate, especially in scenarios with high correlation among interfering transmissions. Simulations were conducted to confirm the analytical findings and demonstrate the superior performance of the designed coding method over standard methods. This research was inspired by recent advancements in wireless data transmission over electromagnetic waves, as seen in examples such as Wi-Fi and radio frequency identification (RFID) technology. Specifically, the study was motivated by the observation that electromagnetic waves often exhibit high levels of correlation in local environments, which can lead to the representational collapse phenomenon. To overcome this limitation, a novel coding technique is proposed, which effectively reduces the effects of representational collapse and achieves superior performance in scenarios with high correlation among interfering transmissions. This research has the potential to open new avenues in the development of coding methods for wireless data transmission, which can be applied to a wide range of fields including IoT, Wi-Fi, and RF technology. Additionally, the study provides valuable insights into the performance of deep learning algorithms in wireless communications, highlighting their susceptibility to representational collapse. As a result, the research can be seen as a pioneering effort to bridge the gap between wireless data transmission and deep learning, which holds significant promise for future advancements in this field. Specifically, the study suggests that future research can be directed at exploring the potential of deep learning algorithms in wireless data transmission, particularly in scenarios with high levels of correlation among interfering transmissions, as evidenced by the successful application of the proposed coding method in these scenarios. In video processing, precise identification of key features across frames is essential for achieving high accuracy in recognition tasks.  Although pixel feature learning has been widely utilized in video models, it suffers from a major limitation: it fails to fully exploit spatial correlations within a frame, thus decreasing overall efficiency.  To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach called patchwise feature learning that outperforms pixel feature learning and yields improved results compared to existing techniques.  By dividing each frame into multiple patches, our approach extracts unique features from each patch, thereby enhancing recognition accuracy while reducing computational costs.  Furthermore, we introduce a patch embedding technique that facilitates seamless information sharing between patches, thereby boosting performance.  Experimental results confirm that patchwise feature learning offers superior features over pixel feature learning, resulting in substantial gains in accuracy on challenging benchmark datasets such as ImageNet.  Notably, our approach achieves remarkable accuracy on top of our benchmark, including a remarkable 78.2% top-1 accuracy on Places365-V2 while utilizing significantly fewer parameters compared to state-of-the-art video models.  A detailed analysis of our approach is available on our official GitHub repository.  Additionally, we introduce a novel video benchmark called Video Invariant Network Benchmark (VIB) that assesses a model's ability to resist video-style attacks while maintaining recognition accuracy.  By integrating VIB into our training pipeline, we enhance the robustness of our approach, thereby significantly decreasing vulnerability to video attacks while increasing overall accuracy.  Specifically, our approach achieves a remarkable 79.6% top-1 accuracy on Places365-V2 while exhibiting exceptional resistance to video attacks, thereby solidifying our approach as a leading solution in this domain. We examine the one-dimensional discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process with periodic boundaries, using parallel updates rules. For a specific type of update, we show that the quench dynamics can be mapped to a particle dynamics process. This mapping allows us to apply an exact method from a different context to investigate the quench dynamics. As a result, we find the exact average density and the exact calculation of the covariance matrix at any given time, for any initial condition, even though individual particle paths are difficult to follow. Notably, this finding provides a direct method to calculate the local probability distribution of a particle at any time, which is a challenging problem in the general case, especially when only numerical results can be obtained. In addition to these general outcomes, we also identify specific limits for the average density, the variance, and the specific joint probability distribution of two particles at large time, given specific initial conditions. These general and specific outcomes are verified by comparing them with existing exact results derived using different methods. Furthermore, we present numerical predictions that can potentially be verified or disproved in the semi-infinite version of the process. The relationship between the present exact method and the original Ginzburg-Landau theory is also explored. In addition, we present numerical results that demonstrate the breakdown of the Ginzburg-Landau theory at large time in the semi-infinite version of the process. The present exact method appears to be the first to calculate the local probability distribution of a particle at any time, making it a valuable tool for testing theoretical predictions. It can also be applied to other processes that are difficult to study directly. In this study, we present a novel method for generating complex, low-frequency microwave patterns using an on-chip optomechanical device. The mechanical oscillator within a parallel RLC circuit engages with both electrical components, effectively creating an analog computational element. We demonstrate the creation of intricate, pseudo-periodic patterns and their ability to produce pseudo-Morse and pseudo-Lorentzian shapes. Additionally, we showcase the generation of low-frequency, pseudo-sinusoidal patterns, exemplifying the potential for wide-ranging frequency coverage. Notably, this scheme offers a planar, autonomous, and energy-efficient mechanism for generating diverse microwave patterns. Due to its mechanical underpinnings, it possesses inherent frequency tunability and can be easily integrated with other optomechanical devices. Therefore, this method holds significant potential for applications in analog computing and novel optomechanical device designs. Furthermore, we outline a broader vision for optomechanics to contribute to advancements in general analog computing technologies. Lastly, we suggest potential future research directions for this field.

Surgical training for laparoscopic procedures is complex and demanding due to the limitations of the surgical field's view. A technique called desmoking has been developed to create a smoke-free environment, allowing for better visibility. Analyzing the smoke patterns can be challenging due to their similarity to the surgery itself. Our research proposes an automated approach to desmoking by tracking the smoke patterns using an unsupervised clustering method and optimizing the laparoscope position for maximum smoke removal. This technique has been successfully validated in two surgical centers with different surgical tools and operates distinctly from existing methods. Our experiments showed a significant decrease in the time it took to start surgery once the smoke-free environment was created. Specifically, the time reduced from an average of 25 seconds to between 8-12 seconds. Additionally, our method demonstrated smoke removal efficiency rates of 85-90% and was found to be compatible with various surgical tools and environments. These results indicate that this approach can be an effective solution for creating a smoke-free environment during laparoscopic surgeries. Our source code is available online at: \href{https://github.com/IVRL-UNSW/Desmoking}{https://github.com/IVRL-UNSW/Desmoking} for further evaluation by the medical community. Future work will focus on incorporating clinical performance metrics to assess the overall success of the desmoking process. These metrics will include the duration of the procedure, the amount of smoke removed, patient comfort, and the ease with which surgical tools can be used. By incorporating these factors, we can develop a more comprehensive evaluation of the desmoking process that goes beyond mere technical assessment. Ultimately, these efforts aim to contribute to the development of effective smoke removal methods that not only improve surgical outcomes but also facilitate training for the next generation of surgeons. Our research is currently ongoing and the findings will be presented at the \emph{International Conference on Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery} in Berlin, Germany. Through advanced computational methods, we have thoroughly examined the structure of paraelectric barium titanate, a material widely studied due to its properties and potential in modeling similar perovskites. Our investigation revealed that the most stable configuration of this material corresponds to a distorted version of the ideal cubic structure, comprising regions of TiO$_3$ and BaO layers arranged in specific patterns. These distortions are driven by specific vibrational modes that are inherent in the material's phonon spectrum. Additionally, we have identified a new structural feature, which gives rise to long-range polar correlations in the material's bulk phase, thus influencing its macroscopic properties and behavior. These findings provide valuable insights into the material's internal workings and can be applied to model similar materials. Finally, our study highlights the significance of accurately modeling the material's phonon spectrum in predicting its properties.

Machine learning methods for analyzing complex, multi-part data are developing rapidly, yet there's a lack of corresponding tools for studying intricate data composed of many components. This gap is hindering research in fields like medicine and social sciences, where such data frequently arises. We address this issue by creating new statistical models that can effectively handle high dimensions and capture meaningful relationships within such data. By utilizing the inherent smoothness of such data, we derive efficient estimation techniques and establish their performance guarantees, even in large data sets. Our approach also enables the detection of significant changes over time or across different groups. We apply our methodology successfully to real-world problems, including tracking blood flow changes in the brain over time and identifying age-related alterations in brain connectivity. Our findings reveal substantial insights and confirm previous studies' key discoveries. Our comprehensive software framework is available for public use. 

Our models for capturing the intrinsic connections within such data are inspired by Gaussian graphical models and utilize a combination of sparse regularization and the Charlier decomposition. This leads to novel formulations that effectively handle the unique characteristics of such data and enable the efficient recovery of both the underlying relationships and any changes that occur. Currently available quantum processors are subject to errors and have limited coherence. To overcome this limitation, researchers employ advanced methods to correct errors, such as noise filtering and reward systems. Nevertheless, these approaches require significant quantitative experience, which is not feasible given the short lifespan of quantum coherence. Our study focuses on developing effective strategies to optimize algorithm performance on short-lived quantum processors. We utilized a simulated quantum processor to investigate the performance of the Grover algorithm with varying error rates. The results indicate that selecting the next gate based on the current state, rather than randomly, is the most effective approach. This strategy outperforms alternative methods, such as choosing the next gate randomly or simultaneously, and can even improve performance after errors have been introduced. To facilitate practical application, we also developed a simple and efficient algorithm for selecting the best gate based on past states, which yields nearly the same performance as the optimal approach. This finding has potential implications for improving quantum algorithm execution. Additionally, our work is accessible through a public repository for use in other algorithms. Finally, our research demonstrates that even short-lived quantum processors can excel at certain search algorithms, achieving speeds up to 3.35 classical computers. This speedup can be achieved with error rates exceeding 90%, and may be feasible with upcoming middle-scale quantum processors. A substantial number of intelligent systems are put into practice, yet due to their complexity, it is difficult to predict all possible errors they might make. Consequently, a mechanism is needed to gather information about any mistakes they do. This information can then be used to create safer and more reliable systems. This paper explores strategies for gathering and learning from reports of incidents that have actually occurred. We find that while there are many methods for gathering data, there isn't much thought given to the part where you actually use that data to improve performance. This is especially true when working with unstructured data, which presents its own set of challenges. After reviewing the various approaches that have been tried, we identify some key areas of improvement and outline some potential future directions, such as making these processes more automated and allowing them to be applied in situations where there aren't many examples available. Ultimately, we conclude by highlighting some of the fundamental questions that need to be answered in order to make progress in this field. This work was presented at IJCAI 21 as a panel discussion and is now being published as a report that summarizes the key points and ideas discussed. The full text is included in the appendix as well.

The principle underlying the renormalization group bears a strong analogy to gradient flow, especially in scalar field theory where the RG and gradient flows share a direct connection through the ERG formalism. This correspondence is rooted in the fact that the ERG is applicable to any quantum field theory, whereas gradient flow is confined to perturbative field theory. This report explores the ERG formulation in dimensionally reduced Yang--Mills theory, allowing for a direct comparison of renormalization group and gradient flow in a non-trivial setting. The findings reveal that the ERG can be recast as a RG equation that is analogous to the parabolic equation governing the Wilson flow in the renormalized gauge theory. However, the correspondence between the RG and gradient flows is limited as the parabolic equation is only applicable in dimensional reduction and does not generalize to other renormalization schemes. Furthermore, the report identifies a key difference in the applicability of the RG and gradient flows, stemming from the fact that the latter relies on the presence of a mass term, whereas the former can operate at zero mass or with a non-zero momentum-dependent mass. Additionally, the report examines the interplay between the RG and gradient flows in the context of the non-perturbative flow equation derived from the ERG, which reveals a distinct distinction between the renormalization group and gradient flows. While the RG equation provides a framework for analyzing the ultraviolet behavior of the theory, the gradient flow parabolic equation is inextricably linked to the presence of an IR cutoff. Consequently, any non-trivial non-perturbative solution of the gradient flow equation will inevitably introduce an IR cutoff, thereby precluding the possibility of a non-perturbative ERG solution that is both UV completion and free from IR cutoffs. This report concludes by highlighting the key distinctions between the RG and gradient flows in non-perturbative quantum field theories, emphasizing the crucial role of the ERG in providing a framework for analyzing the non-perturbative renormalization group behavior in dimensional reduction. While the gradient flow parabolic equation is pivotal in the perturbative context, its applicability is severely limited in the non-perturbative regime due to its inextricable link with an IR cutoff. Quipper, a widely used quantum programming language, has been enhanced with a novel type system that caters to linear types. This improvement builds upon existing research in functional programming, adapting techniques such as the Howard correspondence and linear lambda calculus to accommodate quantum-specific concepts. The updated type system aligns with the structural recursion paradigm, allowing for a straightforward definition of type equations. Additionally, this article describes how the existing algorithm for type inference is modified to support the refined type system. Due to potential conflicts between linear types and the need for sharing in quantum circuits, the implementation includes novel handling methods. A custom interpreter and compiler have been developed to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed type system, with the source code made available on GitHub. Testing showed that the majority of existing Quipper projects can be successfully compiled with the extended type system, and a few common benchmarks demonstrated a minor performance decrease. However, as a result of the linear approach, compile-time errors are now detected earlier compared to the previous system. Polynomial-time reduction methods, referred to as kernelization algorithms, decrease the size of problems within a predetermined limit. Specifically, these algorithms either produce a subset of at most $k$ elements or an instance within a predetermined size limit. Research has shown that for various combinatorial optimization problems, there are upper bounds on how much an instance can be reduced, characterized by a function of $n$ and $k$. On the other hand, there are lower bounds on how much an instance can be reduced, also characterized by a function of $n$ and $k$. These lower bounds are often achieved through the creation of 'hard' instances, which are artificially constructed to be resistant to kernelization. In the context of fundamental optimization problems, it is often desired to determine whether such kernelization methods exist. In this study, we explore the creation of artificially constructed instances that are resistant to kernelization in the context of the Clique problem. Our findings indicate that for the Clique problem with a fixed target clique size, there exist instances that cannot be reduced in size and will always contain at least $k^n$ edges, confirming a long-held conjecture. Our research also extends the existing lower bounds for the Minimum Independent Dominating Set problem and the k-Clustering problem. We introduce a new efficient approach for representing functions in graphical models, taking advantage of the lower memory requirements of deterministic finite state automata (DFAs) compared to standard data structures. This method enables the potential for significant memory savings, particularly beneficial for models involving large functions and limited computational resources. Our major contributions are a reliable algorithm for constructing the DFA from a function and a reliable method for evaluating a DFA on input data, both of which operate within a polynomial time complexity relative to the size of the function. We also demonstrate that our proposed approach is adaptable to parallel processing, enabling substantial speed improvements on multi-core systems. Experimental results confirm the high scalability of our deterministic approach, surpassing the performance of alternative methods in several key benchmarks. This contribution has the potential to benefit numerous applications employing graphical models, particularly those on resource-constrained embedded devices. Graphical models are fundamental to numerous machine learning applications, including structured prediction tasks in areas like computer vision, natural language processing, and structured prediction, where functions are used to define constraints and objectives.
