This study examines the current state of computations for electroweak and mixed electroweak-QCD corrections, specifically at the three-loop order. Calculations of this complexity have become necessary to achieve precise predictions in modern particle physics, crucial for analyzing precise data from particle accelerators. While breakthroughs in massless calculations using algebraic methods are significant, tackling the fully massive case remains an intractable problem using these methods. We explore alternative approaches that utilize differential equations in combination with sector decomposition to facilitate three-loop calculations in massive form. Sector decomposition is shown to efficiently handle these complex computations, allowing us to derive sector-decomposed differential equations for various master integrals even in situations where the full massive representation seems intractable. We also develop a universal procedure for sector-decomposing differential equations and outline a strategy for systematically resolving three-loop corrections. We provide concrete sector-decomposed differential equations for two specific examples, and our results include the complete three-loop corrections to the $\rho$-parameter in the Standard Model for different momentum and mass configurations. We further apply this approach to compute the fully massive four-loop corrections to the $O_{1,2}$ oblique parameters. We verify our results by comparing them with independent calculations using other methods. Additionally, we use these results to derive four-loop corrections to the electroweak mixing angle in the Fermilab representation and to the $\Delta\rho$ parameter at four-loop order, including both electroweak and QCD corrections. We also derive four-loop corrections to the $\Delta\rho$ parameter at four-loop order, applicable to various mass scenarios. Furthermore, we use these results to derive four-loop constraints on the electroweak mixing angle under different mass configurations, including the case where all three fermion masses are non-zero. These calculations also enable us to analyze the momentum dependence of the electroweak mixing angle in various mass scenarios. Our research examines how structural irregularities influence the valley Hall behavior in two-dimensional materials. Utilizing a semi-classical model and considering both static and dynamic strains, we analyze the effect on the valley Hall response. Notably, static strain has a significant impact, causing the valley Hall effect to reverse its direction within a particular strain range. Additionally, we identify the underlying mechanism in an ideal crystal lattice and further investigate how valence band maxima and conduction band minima respond to strain in a realistic scenario. Finally, we apply our model to HfO$_2$/MoS$_2$ heterostructures and demonstrate the control of valley states by strain. This finding has potential implications for the development of strain-controlled, two-dimensional devices.

A key benefit is that digital-analog methods allow classical inputs to produce quantum outputs, giving a significant computational edge. However, the potential of these methods is limited by the understanding of how to effectively use their digital-analog resources.

Focusing on simulating fermionic behavior, a crucial aspect of chemistry, we found that a fully connected qubit arrangement achieves the best results using digital-analog methods. Furthermore, we developed a new way to determine the optimal circuit complexity needed for fermionic simulation, one that significantly outperforms previous digital-analog applications and sets a new standard.

Our work also shows that digital-analog methods excel in solving maximally entangled vertex cover problems, a challenging task in analog quantum computing. This discovery opens up new possibilities for using digital-analog resources in a wide range of algorithms. Overall, our research indicates that digital-analog methods have considerable potential in digital-analog computing. 

Finally, we applied the same digital-analog logic to enhance maximum multipartite entanglement, achieving unprecedented results and revealing novel applications for digital-analog methods in enhancing quantum connectivity. This advancement has the potential to revolutionize quantum technology. 

In conclusion, our research demonstrates that digital-analog methods offer a wealth of new computational opportunities, from complex chemical simulations to groundbreaking quantum connections. These opportunities are now available and can be leveraged to drive progress in quantum computing.

A common issue with initializing deep neural networks is that random starting points often lead to suboptimal performance. Research has demonstrated that initiating networks with structured, high-level representations can expedite optimization and enhance generalization. Nonetheless, developing universal initialization methods remains an unresolved problem. In this research, we introduce a novel approach called Multi-Scale Feature Embedding (MFE) that enables the creation of rich, multi-scale features for neural network initialization. MFE integrates diverse features at various spatial or temporal scales, which can be applied to various network architectures and datasets. We have thoroughly tested MFE on numerous benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10/Cifar-100, Tiny ImageNet, and EMNIST-64, in comparison to leading baseline methods. Notably, MFE has consistently outperformed existing benchmark initialization techniques, achieving superior performance in a reduced training time of 20-50\% less than baseline methods on various datasets. Furthermore, MFE has successfully enhanced the performance of several popular networks, including ResNet, Wide ResNet, and MobileNet, on image classification tasks. In addition to its optimization benefits, MFE has also been found to boost the robustness of neural networks against adversarial attacks. In light of its outstanding performance and versatility, we propose MFE as a universal initialization technique suitable for a wide range of deep neural networks. Achieving the formation of a precise, stable spot in turbid media is a difficult task due to random light scattering. Scattering disrupts the coherent signal from the source, replacing it with a bright ring and a darker center, which is often undesirable. We've developed a new method using an adaptive optics system that utilizes a MEMS wavefront sensor and an SLM to correct wavefront errors in turbid media. Our research showcases the successful implementation of this system in a bovine eye model, accurately placing a 5.54 micron spot even at depths of 3.25 mm. Additionally, we've refined the available computational techniques to enhance the image quality and accuracy in scattering media, combining these methods with adaptive optics to reach a level of diffraction-limit in a 3D environment. Our findings demonstrate the potential for using adaptive optics in 3D imaging of large biological objects.

By utilizing this data, we can effectively normalize comparisons and identify a suitable reward function, leading to accurate performance assessment. The approach is continuous-time and can be implemented in both batch and online settings, with a theoretical time complexity of $O(N^{-4/\alpha}\mathrm{log}^3 N)$ for the former and $O(T^{-2\alpha/(2+\alpha)})$ for the latter, where $N$ or $T$ represents the amount of available data. Furthermore, we show that our method outperforms existing approaches in a range of experiments. 

A key challenge in achieving this performance lies in leveraging the data from the testing distribution without relying on knowledge of its distribution function. We address this issue by employing a continuous-time kernel-based operator that generalizes known results from the statistical learning theory. 

The proposed method has practical applications in at least two scenarios. Firstly, it can be used when data from the testing distribution becomes available during the training process in predictive regimes. Secondly, it offers an efficient alternative to counterfactual reasoning, which typically involves two separate policy evaluations – one for initial and another for counterfactual policy assessment. By integrating data from the testing distribution into policy learning, we can eliminate the need for these separate evaluations and instead perform a single cross-validation to assess the counterfactual policy.

This paper examines the performance of cluster-robust variance-covariance estimators in meta-analyses, particularly when the number of studies is limited. We show that while these estimators can handle arbitrary study correlations, they are prone to extreme variability when the number of studies is small. This issue is particularly evident in weighted analyses and can lead to inaccurate confidence intervals and false positive results. We identify two main sources of this variability: the zero-variance problem and the correlation amplification effect, both of which are more pronounced in weighted analyses. We also find that the cluster-bootstrap solution is ineffective in addressing these challenges when the number of studies is small. To mitigate these problems, we propose an alternative cluster-robust variance-covariance estimator that is derived using a unbiased estimator of the weighted average difference. Notably, this new estimator exhibits improved performance in terms of precision and accuracy, particularly when the number of studies is small. We also find that the cluster-robust weighted diploid and cluster-bootstrap solutions often produce wider confidence intervals compared to our proposed estimator. When applied to real-world meta-analyses, our proposed estimator resulted in more conservative conclusions compared to the original cluster-robust and cluster-bootstrap approaches. The findings of this study highlight the importance of carefully evaluating the performance of statistical methods before implementing them in practice. The code and data used in this research are freely available for reproduction.

A widely adopted integration method for simulating particle collisions is the Variable Time Step (VTS) algorithm, which uses a collision time calculation algorithm. This method accelerates simulations by eliminating unnecessary collision resolutions. However, the traditional VTS algorithm speeds up collisions, but also introduces errors such as stretching collision time, which can lead to untrustworthy simulations. This research extends the VTS algorithm for particle simulations, incorporating a collision duration adjustment factor. This modified algorithm, the Enhanced VTS (EVTS), accurately handles particle collisions within a shorter time frame. Additionally, the study evaluates the EVTS algorithm's impact on sediment transport simulations using a parallel computing environment. The results show that using the EVTS algorithm yields results comparable to the exact integration method, but with significantly faster computation times. For instance, the EVTS algorithm speeds up simulations by factors of 2.45 and 2.13 when modeling riverbed sedimentation and erosion, respectively. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the EVTS algorithm can efficiently handle large-scale simulations on a parallel computing platform, delivering faster results than the exact integration method. Based on these findings, the EVTS algorithm offers a reliable and efficient solution for simulating particle collisions and can be effectively applied to a wide range of complex particle sedimentation and erosion problems in various environments. These scenarios include the movement of sediment in water or air, the collapse of volcanic ash, or the explosion of explosive materials. The research provides a valuable approach for accurately modeling particle collisions in a computationally efficient manner. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information structures. Presently, most techniques represent information as a flat list or a simple tree structure; however, these representations fall short in capturing relationships for items further down the list. In contrast, this research introduces a new model that uses a balance of hierarchical grouping and interconnectedness to represent information. The proposed framework relies on hierarchical clustering and simulates relationships between grouped items to maintain consistency with the hierarchical structure. It offers flexible control over the trade-off between grouping intensity and the depth of the hierarchy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this new approach using two real-world datasets, comparing its accuracy to other existing methods. Additionally, we show that our model enables the detection of patterns within the data that were previously inaccessible. When software modifications introduce a high risk of bugs, it's crucial to prioritize testing immediately. Typically, a comprehensive suite of tests is conducted initially, followed by subsequent testing of individual components as issues arise. This differs from the standard approach of performing a full suite run each time changes are made. We've developed an innovative strategy, risk-driven incremental testing, which swiftly assesses high-risk code changes and guarantees thorough testing of all modifications. Through an extensive examination of 35 software projects at GitHub, our results indicate that this method enhances testing efficiency by an average of 40% compared to the standard incremental approach and yields comparable coverage to the full suite method. Our proposed technique is now freely available on GitHub. https://github.com/SoftwareEngineeringResearchGroup/RISKDT.git. A novel deep learning approach is developed to forecast suicidal ideation based on combined Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data. Research indicates that integrating multiple data sources enhances the prediction of complex mental health conditions. This study leverages a combined dataset of EHR and EMA, treating the latter as time-series data to predict suicidal ideation. We demonstrate that incorporating EMA records elevates the prediction accuracy of suicidal ideation when utilizing only EHR data. Furthermore, we investigate the optimal integration strategies for forecasting suicidal ideation from both EHR and EMA data. Experimental outcomes using three distinct loss functions confirm that a two-task learning framework yields the highest accuracy in predicting suicidal ideation compared to singular task models. We also examine the performance of various neural network architectures, revealing that a bidirectional attention-based model exhibits superior results, surpassing state-of-the-art methods. We validate our approach through rigorous cross-validation and thorough ablation studies on a real-world dataset, ultimately achieving a high Area under the ROC curve of 0.890. We anticipate this research will contribute to the advancement of deep learning methods in forecasting suicidal ideation. A recent study of the Cassiopeia A supernova remnant was conducted using Chandra observations from 2016. The X-ray emission was categorized into three distinct components: synchrotron radiation, reverse shock emission, and forward shock emission. The analysis revealed an asymmetry in the synchrotron component, primarily caused by a discrepancy in the count rates between the northeast and northwest regions. By comparing this finding to a previous observation from 2000, it was determined that the polarization degree of the synchrotron radiation has a median value of approximately 0.23 across the eastern and western edges of the remnant. The researchers also identified a potential forward shock emission for the first time and calculated its X-ray temperature to be around 0.64 keV. Furthermore, they estimated a mass of approximately 1.38 solar masses for the central neutron star based on its X-ray luminosity. The study provided constraints on the energy distribution of cosmic-ray electrons, showing that the measured polarization degree is in agreement with models of magnetic field topology and electron energy spectrum. The findings of this research contribute to our understanding of particle acceleration in supernova remnants. The research also laid the groundwork for further studies of the polarization degree of the synchrotron radiation as the remnant expands and its surface magnetic field becomes more disordered. The expected decrease in polarization degree is anticipated to be relatively slow, around a percent per thousand years over the next ten thousand years. The research further suggests that a significant factor influencing the future polarization degree will be the continued growth of the forward shock emission. If this trend continues, it is possible that the polarization degree of the synchrotron radiation could eventually dominate the X-ray emission of Cassiopeia A, leading to a potential misidentification of its physical properties. The research concludes by highlighting the importance of continued monitoring of the polarization degree as the remnant expands and evolves. The potential for future X-ray telescopes with greater sensitivity and better spatial resolution to uncover new physical phenomena in Cassiopeia A is also explored. The research further suggests that a future all-sky polarization-sensitive X-ray survey could reveal many more supernova remnants like Cassiopeia A, offering a unique opportunity to study the evolution of cosmic ray acceleration and the magnetic field topology. A three-dimensional topological insulator exhibits a distinctive response to an electric potential that varies across space, characterized by a non-zero total current except when time-reversal symmetry is observed, in which case it remains zero. This property can be utilized to quantify a time-reversal symmetry-protected insulator's topological characteristics by measuring the electric potential and resulting electromagnetic fields across the entire material volume. This concept is applied to a specific model of a time-reversal symmetry-protected insulator, consisting of three layers with distinct electric potentials, to demonstrate that the material exhibits a 1/2 charge per unit cell from both the electric potential and resulting electromagnetic fields. Furthermore, the model shows that the material's topological characteristics can be altered by adjusting the difference in electric potentials between two particular layers, leading to a continuous transformation between a topological insulator and a trivial insulator phases. This model represents a three-dimensional equivalent of the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect, offering potential applications in the creation of a room-temperature electronic channel protected by time-reversal symmetry for the study and utilization of topological characteristics. Additionally, the material's properties suggest the existence of a previously unknown phase, characterized by a surface protected by time-reversal symmetry and featuring both gapped and gapless regions due to the presence of counter-propagating electronic waves. This new phase may hold significance in the study and utilization of topological characteristics, potentially through the use of a tunneling gapless state into a fully gapped state to control a electronic channel protected by time-reversal symmetry. Finally, the model's properties indicate that the material's topological characteristics can be observed not only on its surface but also throughout its entire volume by adjusting the electric potential and resulting electromagnetic fields. This phenomenon is attributed to the material's time-reversal symmetry-protected insulator properties, suggesting a novel approach to studying and utilizing topological characteristics in a three-dimensional system. This research contributes to the existing understanding of topological characteristics, potentially paving the way for innovative applications in electronic devices. In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a rule rather than exception. This research focuses on how the time delay's periodic fluctuation affects a typical nonlinear dynamical system, revealing that such modulation can significantly enhance chaos. We demonstrate that, for certain parameters, periodic modulation of the time delay leads to a substantial increase in the area of the chaotic attractor, a phenomenon that also occurs in other types of complex dynamics, such as the butterfly effect. Notably, this effect is observed in a large number of systems and can be implemented using the well-known Lorenz system through variable air-filled delay tubes. Importantly, we show that these findings are not limited to theoretical models, but can also be replicated in real-world systems through accurate numerical simulations. To achieve this, we developed and tested an innovative method to precisely modulate the time delay in a system of delay tubes. This work not only expands our understanding of complex dynamics but also enables the development of advanced and robust artificial systems, such as hidden pattern generators and complex oscillators. Furthermore, we propose a novel mechanism for memory storage in digital systems, utilizing complex dynamics' high sensitivity to initial conditions. This approach offers superior performance compared to existing analog memory methods. Finally, we outline a promising direction for future research, exploring the potential for complex dynamics in delay systems to be harnessed for cryptography purposes. Due to its practical implications, this study's findings can contribute significantly to the development of both artificial intelligence and security systems. We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). Furthermore, building on initial research into stochastic typing (Bacci et al., 2019), we explore the possibilities of introducing type systems that can capture both the structural and operational aspects of context-sensitive probability properties in high-level probabilistic code. A key finding is the existence of sound and sufficient type systems for both denotational and operational interpretations. Finally, we confirm that the stochastic lambda calculus with our proposed type systems provides a fully faithful model by proving an adequacy theorem that bridges denotational and operational views with respect to type-correct higher-order probabilistic code. This result is further substantiated by developing a verified interpreter for a type-of-type stochastic lambda calculus and an associated testing framework that validates its soundness through extensive empirical evaluation. Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation purposes. This can be achieved through a process called design mining, which applies machine learning to learn design relevance from examples. We have created a simple and effective model for design mining using comment data from GitHub, which involves no custom programming skills and can be easily adapted by anyone familiar with basic machine learning concepts. This model was trained using a publicly accessible dataset of open-source projects and categorizes sentences as design relevant or irrelevant. We have found that this approach is beneficial in creating valuable documentation for software design, particularly useful when discussions exceed what can be covered in code reviews or change logs. This model is versatile and can be applied to various applications beyond software design, such as identifying relevant information in online comments. Additionally, we provide guidance on implementing design mining for individual projects by analyzing the variation in how different developers engage with design issues. This analysis can aid project maintainers in identifying areas of focus for design-related discussions and potentially even implementing design patterns. We have shared our model and the accompanying analysis through two public repositories to facilitate design mining for individual projects, promoting design knowledge through standardization. This knowledge can then be utilized to enhance design-related discussions, ultimately contributing to better design understanding among developers, which in turn can lead to improved software quality through design-centric development processes. To date, we have applied our model to eight widely-used open-source projects, revealing insights into design discussions, such as common design tools, programming languages used, and the evolution of design issues over time. These insights can be beneficial in guiding design-related discussions and promoting design best practices, as seen in the maintenance of the Linux kernel project. We have made our findings and analysis publicly accessible to encourage design mining for individual projects, promoting design knowledge through standardization. This knowledge can then be effectively utilized to enhance design understanding among developers, ultimately contributing to better design and improved software quality through design-centric development processes. To facilitate design mining for individual projects, we have created a step-by-step tutorial, including necessary code snippets, to aid project maintainers in replicating our analysis. We hope this initiative inspires a community of researchers to engage in design mining to gain insights into software design, shedding new light on existing knowledge through collaborative analysis. We envision a future where design mining contributes significantly to our understanding of software design, promoting design best practices, and ultimately leading to improved software quality through design-centric development processes. A new theory proposes that gravity, dark energy, and dark matter are three facets of a single phenomenon resulting from nearly uniform, very spread-out negative pressure within the vacuum. This pressure, caused by an excessive superposition of positive and negative energy states at the zero-point energy level, gives rise to the observed high zero-point energy density. A fundamental aspect of this theory is that gravity is a gradual outcome of the inhomogeneous gradient of the zero-point energy density. This theory's framework offers a coherent understanding of dark energy and dark matter, revealing them to be the dual manifestations of the inhomogeneous zero-point energy density characteristic of the vacuum state. By examining the spatial distribution of this density, one can identify regions where the negative pressure is particularly low, giving rise to the observed phenomenon of gravitation. Furthermore, the theory explains why this phenomenon appears localized rather than dispersed. A critical component of the theory involves the concept of "critical density," which serves as a threshold for distinguishing between regions of vacuum instability associated with matter and those associated with radiation. A crucial empirical test of the theory can be performed by investigating the vacuum energy density and its relationship with the Hubble constant at the cosmic scale. Additionally, the theory suggests that the density fluctuations resulting from this process could plausibly account for the observed abundance of dark matter. Importantly, the theory does not imply the creation of matter from the vacuum; rather, it posits that matter is a byproduct of the spatial distribution of existing zero-point energy fluctuations. This distinction is significant, as it allows the theory to sidestep the long-standing issues of particle antimatter parity and the conservation of fermion number. A notable feature of this theory is its ability to resolve the long-standing Hubble tension through a natural discrepancy between the vacuum energy density and the density required to match the Hubble constant. Finally, the theory offers an innovative explanation for the observed phenomenon of gravitational waves, proposing that these waves are a manifestation of the dynamic movement of energy density fluctuations within the vacuum. This entanglement is a universal property of all gravitational waves and has profound implications for our understanding of the fundamental nature of gravity. A new class of proximal gradient algorithms has been developed for nonsmooth, differentiable problems with constraints. These constraints can be enforced via augmented Lagrangian methods, but the gradient of the Lagrangian may not exist, making it difficult to apply traditional methods. The proposed algorithms overcome this challenge by using the existence of the gradient for the differentiable part and the proximal method's ability to utilize the properties of the nonsmooth part, even in the presence of inexact penalty terms. This approach enables the development of efficient, convergent algorithms for various nonsmooth, differentiable optimization problems with equality and inequality constraints. We define a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a commutative ring with identity as an ideal that, when divided by any non-zero element, results in either a zero or a product of two elements. Our main aim in this study is to investigate these types of ideals in relation to syndetic sets within a commutative ring. Additionally, we establish a correspondence between weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and certain kinds of syndetic sets, as well as examining the unique characteristics of such ideals in specific rings. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of a weakly $1$-absorbing primary ideal and establish its properties in relation to products of elements. This study also delves into specific types of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals known as $\gamma$-weakly $1$-absorbing prime, yielding interesting results on their presence in certain rings. Interestingly, our investigation shows that every ring contains an ideal that is both $\gamma$-weakly $1$-absorbing prime and also fails to meet an even stricter criterion, known as $\gamma$-weakly $2$-absorbing prime. We conclude our study by computing the upper limit for the number of $\gamma$-weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals in a specific type of ring with a finite number of elements. We present new findings for two semileptonic decay processes, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, utilizing data from Belle II. Within a total luminosity of 189.6 inverse femtobarns, and a statistical sample of 85.3 inverse femtobarns after background subtraction, we calculate the branching fractions for these decays. The results show a branching fraction of $(4.41\pm0.29\pm0.18)\times10^{-4}$ for $B^0$ into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair, and $(2.35\pm0.10\pm0.09)\times10^{-4}$ for $B^+$ into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, with the quoted uncertainties representing experimental and theoretical precision respectively. Additionally, we report the first observation of the rare semileptonic decay $B^0$ into $\pi^0$ and a lepton-neutrino pair with a branching fraction of $(0.66\pm0.09\pm0.06)\times10^{-5}$. This finding aligns with the standard model's prediction at the $(3.0\pm0.4)\times10^{-5}$ level of precision. Furthermore, we report no evidence for the decay $B^+$ into $\pi^0$ and a lepton-neutrino pair with a limit of upper limit at the $(2.4\pm0.8\pm0.3)\times10^{-5}$ confidence level, which remains below the standard model's predicted value of $(0.84\pm0.10)\times10^{-5}$. Lastly, we report the measurement of the total branching fraction for the decay $B^0$ into $\tau$-particles along with hadrons, which is found to be $(7.9\pm0.6\pm0.3)\times10^{-4}$, with the quoted uncertainties representing experimental and theoretical precision respectively. This result is in agreement with the standard model's predicted value of $(5.6\pm0.3)\times10^{-4}$. In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged that aim to address polypharmacy problems such as optimizing medication combinations, predicting adverse effects, and identifying effective treatment regimens. However, there's a lack of comprehensive reviews that provide a clear overview of the models, methods, and data employed in these studies. This article aims to fill this gap by examining the application of machine learning in polypharmacy, focusing on the use of models to analyze electronic health records. We'll be examining how machine learning models can utilize the unique characteristics of EHR data, such as sparse and multivariate data, to improve performance. This review also highlights ongoing challenges and potential avenues for future research, along with suggesting essential criteria for evaluating model performance. Furthermore, we'll be discussing potential applications of machine learning in real-world settings and highlighting the need for more transparent and interpretable models that can facilitate better decision-making in healthcare. By covering key aspects such as model evaluation, essential dataset components, and crucial research gaps, this review aims to facilitate further research in this field and contribute to the development of more effective machine learning algorithms for addressing polypharmacy. Additionally, we've created a comprehensive repository that includes a detailed analysis of the discussed topics and provides a unified view of the literature on machine learning for polypharmacy. This repository is accessible at: https://github.com/krishanmdeepte/polypharmacy-machinlearning.

Several local authorities face hurdles in introducing automated assessment of road conditions due to a lack of necessary expertise, high setup costs associated with collecting and processing data, and limited availability of suitable infrastructure. While some successful applications of machine learning have been observed, they often necessitate access to large quantities of already collected data, a scenario that rarely occurs in these cases. This study aims to explore the potential of using only a minimal amount of just 50 gathered images to train an accurate model for detecting and classifying cracks in roads. To achieve this, it employs a novel self-supervised method called SelfAided Pseudo-Labeling with Mixed-Mode (SAPM) training, combining traditional supervised learning with the incorporation of pseudo-labeled data produced through self-supervised encoding. The results, obtained using data collected from four different cities in Germany, indicate that this approach outperforms conventional methods by a substantial margin, with the highest overall performance being 94% in terms of the F1 score. Notably, this technique exhibits particular strength in handling sparse data scenarios, making it extremely beneficial for local authorities with limited available resources. Imitation learning seeks to bypass the difficulty of creating suitable reward functions by training agents to mimic expert behavior. While this approach is appealing, providing a large dataset of expert actions is often impractical due to the expense and complexity of gathering such data. This problem is particularly prevalent in the training of mobile manipulator agents, where generating diverse trajectories requires significant effort. To overcome this limitation, we propose a method to learn these trajectories by analyzing the structure of the mobile manipulator's configuration space. This involves partitioning the space into distinct regions and learning an imitation policy within each area separately. As a result, we achieve better performance when comparing the current approach to a traditional method of breaking down the training process into separate components for planning and control. Our method shows promise by successfully applying it to a mobile manipulator learning to pour tea, a complex task that requires considerable skill. Overall, we demonstrate that mobile manipulator imitators can be efficiently trained to perform a range of tasks in various environments while also increasing the versatility of mobile manipulator learning. The early universe's protostar formation is a complex process, and our understanding of it is limited by the lack of precise data on key factors, such as magnetic field behavior during the star formation process. In a recent study, researchers have developed a new approach to simulate this process in a controlled environment. They found that even within a controlled setup, magnetic field amplification follows a predictable pattern, strengthening by two orders of magnitude through differential rotation within the first two years. This rapid growth significantly enhances the formation of secondary protostars in the early universe, and their numbers could reach up to ten thousand, given typical early universe conditions. This extensive protostar formation would likely last for a few years, after which the magnetic field would become too weak to support further star formation through fragmentation. The rapid evolution of protostars in the early universe's cosmological magnetic field could leave lasting imprints on the early universe's cosmic structure, affecting the formation of the first galaxies. The findings of this study have important implications for the early universe's cosmological magnetic field's overall impact, and its effects should be considered in future simulations of the early universe's cosmological structure and galaxy formation. Association rule mining aims to uncover relationships between items within transactions, governed by confidence and support criteria. Due to data unpredictability and the absence of a predefined scale, inferring the number of required transactions becomes a challenging task. A common approach involves leveraging statistical inference to estimate this number, with resulting methods outlined in research papers frequently omitting essential implementation details. To address this gap, we provide a clear implementation of two such estimators through a publicly accessible Python repository. Comprehensive testing of these estimators is conducted using various benchmark datasets, with results consisting of both numerical data and visual representations. Achieving accurate predictive models while maintaining users' privacy remains a significant challenge in machine learning. Traditional methods for enforcing differential privacy often rely on eliminating or masking sensitive data, which can lead to inaccurate predictions. In response, this study proposes a novel framework for a private machine learning system based on one-sided differential privacy. This approach, which differs from the established Laplace mechanism, enables more efficient calculation of private gradients without discarding data. We integrated OSDP into a deep learning model, enabling it to achieve accurate classification results while maintaining privacy for individuals and datasets. Notably, this model outperformed a differential privacy-enabled neural network model built using TensorFlow, demonstrating improved accuracy and lower computational costs. Furthermore, we applied and refined this approach in a natural language model, enabling the preservation of privacy for individuals and datasets without compromising its performance. This model achieved comparable results to an non-private version of the same model. This study contributes a novel OSDP analysis for stochastic gradient descent, as well as a practical implementation of a private machine learning system that balances both accuracy and computational complexity. The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, yet dealing with large datasets involving numerous event streams can be extremely challenging due to the high throughput of data generation. This challenge is often referred to as the "event avalanche problem." To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a new approach centered on graph topology, utilizing time-based analysis to filter out irrelevant data and enhance the computation's efficiency by several orders of magnitude, even with thousands of event streams operating simultaneously. The proposed method is thoroughly tested on real-world datasets originating from LHC experiments at CERN, CMB CMBpol, and Cherenkov detector data, showing remarkable improvement in processing capacity and scalability. These findings indicate that this method has great potential for handling the high-throughput data expected from future experiments, including the LHC Phase 2 and AXIONSCOUT. Moreover, we establish that the'mild solution' coincides with the 'weak solution' under both small and large control assumptions. Unlike previous GAN-based methods, which rely on short signal segments, SAGAN operates directly on the entire signal duration. As a result, SAGAN requires a discriminator that can perceive the entire signal, making it feasible through the application of global pooling operations. SAGAN outperforms existing audio generation models in terms of performance, particularly on the task of class-conditional synthesis, while also demonstrating superior performance in the task of frequency classification. Ultimately, this investigation opens up new avenues for the study of high-pressure physics and the development of innovative spintronics technologies. This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a specific class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider the first eigenvalue of the Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem within this domain. We identify both a lower and upper bound for the eigenvalue in question, taking into account the radius $r$ and a measure of the boundary of $\Omega_0$. Notably, our findings indicate that the eigenvalue exhibits a form of asymptotic sparsity similar to recent results obtained through a different approach. Moreover, we show that the contrasts present are the sharpest currently known, achieving a transition from sublinear growth in the lower bound to superlinear growth in the upper bound as the radius $r$ approaches zero. Furthermore, we derive several related results, including a proof that the eigenvalue vanishes as the domain's 'thickness' varies in a certain specified manner, and a demonstration that the eigenvalue remains positive for a particular class of 'thick' domains. To facilitate these findings, we introduce an alternative formulation of the Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem and leverage a careful analysis of a related nonparametric functional. We also utilize a novel combination of weighted Poincaré inequalities to derive the desired bounds and prove the mentioned results. To the best of our knowledge, this research represents an original contribution in the field.}

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometric optics and WKB methods are applied to yield two asymptotic approximations: an inner solution valid near the fluid interface and a supercritical outer solution elsewhere. These approximations are linked using a matching procedure that also facilitates an expansion of the interface deflection as well as the streamfunction in the outer region. Ultimately, both the amplitude and phase components of these quantities exhibit exponential growth or decay, determined by the discriminant of the dispersion relation, with alternating signs due to the sign change of the discriminant. This modeling framework is applied to two instances of laboratory lock-exchange experiments, resulting in a rapid convergence to match within a relatively narrow boundary layer near the interface and excellent agreement with numerical simulations in the outer domain. Consequently, this approach offers a computationally efficient method for modeling such stratified flows with high accuracy. Finally, the implications of this model are extended to analyze the long-term evolution of a river entering the sea. Although initially producing small perturbations to the interface, both the amplitude and phase of the streamfunction eventually exhibit strong exponential growth, leading to the eventual overturning of the ocean-stratified layer and a cataractic interface. Conversely, when only the horizontal viscosity factor is considered, the interface remains smooth and undisturbed. However, when both types of perturbations coexist, an initial period of stability is observed before eventually giving way to exponential growth. Consequently, these findings suggest that the long-term stability of such interfaces is threatened by even the slightest presence of vertical viscosity factors. Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting this type of deception has been
extremely challenging. A novel approach to this problem involves transforming the
issue into a quadratic optimization problem, limited by a solution precision, and
utilizing semidefinite programming to break it down into a manageable linear problem
that can be solved more efficiently. This method has been successfully tested on
real-world examples, outperforming alternative solutions, and yielding results that
can be utilized to inform legal actions against the demonstrated distortions. 
Further research has led to the development of a user-friendly platform for creating,
modifying, and evaluating electoral districts, accessible through a graphical interface,
as well as in command-line and Python variations, and shown its effectiveness in the
analysis of actual districts in North Carolina and Illinois, producing actionable findings. 
This work has culminated in the creation of an open-source CSD library, contributing to
the advancement of the field, as well as launching a website to disseminate research findings
and make the related tools and data available to the public. 
Ultimately, it is hoped that these efforts will lead to the detection and rectification of
gerrymandering in electoral districts, contributing positively to the health of democracy.

and \href{https://dattableg.github.io/CSD/data.html}{dattableg.github.io/CSD/data.html}, respectively.

Researchers have created a mathematical model that describes the electronic behavior near the surface of a Topological Insulator that contains a curved defect - specifically, an edge dislocation. The model reveals that this type of dislocation generates localized areas of unusual electronic activity, known as Dirac cones, that form along the surface of the Topological Insulator in an irregular curved pattern. Additionally, we prove a separate theorem concerning the scarcity of non-constant morphisms towards projective varieties that have a positive height growth rate for the images of the maps, which is a separate theorem in its own right. Robot educators strive to mimic human movement by replicating underlying intentions, but achieving a seamless transition between teaching and imitation proves challenging due to the diverse possibilities of suitable movements. A key factor, known as manipulability, which links joint velocities to object interaction force, offers insight into suitable movements. However, calculating manipulability requires a complex and intricate relationship between joint velocities, making it impractical for widespread use. A more efficient approach has been developed using a simplified method to estimate this relationship, represented by elliptical shapes that illustrate manipulability. This new model is applied to various tasks, including robot teaching, where it facilitates tasks that require specific interaction forces, by assigning rewards to actions within the manipulability ellipse. Additionally, this model successfully replicates human-like movement in tasks that require delicate object handling, by prioritizing force distribution and adjusting joint velocities to maximize manipulability. Successful results from both examples demonstrate the effectiveness of this model, highlighting its potential to streamline complex optimization problems. A comparison of its efficiency to other state-of-the-art methods shows a notable improvement in processing speed. This model has been open-sourced for public use. Estimating a three-dimensional pose from a single image is a complex task because it involves projecting all dimensions into two. Most successful approaches rely on large image datasets linked with 3D object models, but these methods are limited by the need for such connected datasets. Our research reveals that training on pose estimates derived from three-dimensional tracking data within a common framework yields better results than traditional training methods. Moreover, we show that training on the wild, freely available videos offers more accurate estimates than training on carefully controlled and artificially enhanced images. Our framework, dubbed SingleView3D, outperforms the current best approaches by a considerable margin according to the widely used PASCAL3D+ dataset. Additionally, we provide a novel dataset of precise 2D to 3D transformations called PASCAL3D+-T, which significantly improves the performance of all tested methods when used in conjunction with the existing PASCAL3D+ dataset. Our source code and dataset are available for public use at the URL provided in the references.

The COVID-19 pandemic's severity, coupled with the limited time available to develop vaccines, highlight the critical importance of swift immunization efforts.  Despite the extensive scientific validation of these life-saving vaccines, many individuals remain skeptical or misinformed about them.  This research aims to understand the psychological factors driving people's attitudes towards COVID-19 vaccines, with a focus on identifying the influence of social media as a primary information source.  A large-scale online survey was conducted, covering topics such as vaccine acceptance, social media usage, and personal characteristics.  The findings reveal that individuals who rely on social media for information are more likely to reject COVID-19 vaccines, while factors such as health concerns and political affiliations also play a significant role in shaping attitudes.  These results can inform the development of targeted public health campaigns to promote vaccine adoption, highlighting the need to address the spread of misinformation on social media.  Furthermore, this study provides insights into the psychological dynamics underlying the adoption of misinformation, potentially applicable to other public health crises and vaccine prevention efforts.  Finally, this work underscores the significance of balancing individual freedom of information with the responsibility to disseminate accurate information, particularly in the context of public health emergencies.  Such a balance is crucial for mitigating the adverse consequences of social media influence on society.  To this end, this research proposes the utilization of AI-driven information verification tools as a potential means of promoting responsible social media usage and combating the spread of misinformation.  The associated prototype has been made available for public use at https://ai4gov.github.io/COVID-Vaccine-Focus-Group/index.html. This paper investigates the global existence of solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, given initial data with low regularity. It is demonstrated that the solution exhibits exponential decay in both space and time. Notably, the result deviates from the predictions made by the method of almost conservation law, which would suggest the solution's decay only in one dimension. To overcome this limitation, the approach employed involves the use of a novel almost conservation law with a carefully crafted commutator term, integrated by a specially designed flow based on the Littlewood-Paley projector. Additionally, the paper establishes the necessary uniform bounds on the solution and its spatial derivatives, which in turn yields the desired decay estimates. Finally, the method is also applicable to the case of the 2D cubic Schrödinger equation with initial data in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^2)$, resulting in a locally existence and uniqueness theorem. The research provides a new approach to tackling problems with focusing nonlinearity and almost conservation laws. The associated conservation laws are discussed in the appended notes. The methods presented can be extended to address various other nonlinear equations. The paper primarily focuses on the Schrödinger equation, but the techniques are versatile and can be applied to a broader range of problems. This paper presents the findings of a comprehensive analysis of the Rust programming language's Cargo ecosystem in terms of security. Our research focuses on examining the official Cargo packages for potential risks. From a preliminary examination, we identified 324 vulnerabilities in 143 security issues affecting 77 popular Cargo libraries. Our detailed analysis reveals that the most prevalent security threats encountered are typosquatting (account takeover and credential exposure), followed by exploitation of known vulnerabilities inherited from dependencies, and uncovering latent zero-day threats. Our results indicate that Cargo ecosystem security is generally stable but may be susceptible to certain threats. In order to enhance the overall security of Cargo libraries, we recommend that users adopt best practices for dependency management, suggest and implement straightforward security patches, and consider conducting regular security audits. Additionally, Cargo could be enhanced by incorporating automated security checks for libraries during the creation process and by facilitating easy transition to fixed versions of vulnerable dependencies. Our study also introduces TyposquatCargo and SafeCargo, two tools that can detect typosquatting attacks and evaluate the security posture of Cargo libraries, respectively. These tools are available for public use at https://typosquatter.github.io/TyposquatCargo/ and https://typosquatter.github.io/SafeCargo/. Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate energy range are studied using the HADES detector at GSI, Darmstadt, Germany. This collaboration has recently released data on the highest energy setting, which involved a 2.9 GeV incident beam and yielded a substantial sample of 1.7 billion particles. The experiment focused on measuring the production of charged hadrons, particularly at high energy levels where the underlying dynamics start to resemble those of quantum chromodynamics. The measurements encompass a wide range of rapidity and transverse momentum, extending as far as 5 GeV/C and include both light and strange hadrons. The findings are then compared with existing theoretical predictions, which revealed discrepancies in certain cases. The results are further analyzed to investigate the characteristics of final-state interactions and to shed light on the role of transport models in describing this complex phenomenon. The work concludes by outlining suggestions for future investigations that could help clarify the underlying physics of hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate energy range. Deep learning models like Deep Convolutional Neural Networks have significantly revolutionized the field of image recognition, yet they treat images as 2D entities, disregarding their inherent 2.5D nature resulting from light polarization. This characteristic can be leveraged to create more efficient image recognition systems. Our research introduces a novel framework, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), which capitalizes on the diverse properties of light to enhance image understanding and representation capabilities. By incorporating an additional degree of freedom, OCNs outperform traditional state-of-the-art models across various datasets, demonstrating improved accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, we have developed an efficient method for creating a polarization-sensitive image dataset at a relatively low cost, which provides superior performance to standard 2D-based deep learning models. Overall, our proposed framework offers a more effective and efficient approach to image recognition. This study optimizes the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) designed for point cloud learning. We analyze the existing gcn architectures for this purpose and derive a general structure type with multiple stacked layers. Two optimization approaches are proposed to reduce the computational cost: first, a graph construction method is introduced to consolidate multiple gcn layers into one with optimized graph structure; second, a model pruning technique is developed to directly reduce the network size based on the gcn's inherent properties. Both methods are empirically validated on three popular point cloud learning tasks across multiple datasets, demonstrating significant computational savings and minimal performance degradation. Notably, our best model achieves comparable accuracy to the original network while achieving a 73% reduction in computational cost. The source code is available at https://github.com/Chen-Ezki/EEFCN.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack that uses fixed images in trigger formation, making it independent of the class labels and resulting data distributions. Our method employs specifically designed image patterns that can be overlaid on any input, triggering false classifications without affecting the model's performance on clean inputs. Through comprehensive testing on 10 datasets and various models, we demonstrate that our attack method surpasses existing non-data-driven Trojan attacks in terms of accuracy and performance impact, with minimal influence on clean samples, achieving up to 99% success rate and almost no impact on clean samples, making it particularly difficult to detect. We introduce ROSIE, a cutting-edge image dissector for the AAT's 2dF instrument, designed to capture high-quality spectra of up to 112 celestial objects at a resolution of 7000. Our work outlines the technical development, calibration procedures, and initial testing of this new IFU, also describing its operating parameters, including the selection of which objects to observe, and how to align the 2D field of view. Furthermore, we document the steps for reducing the large amount of data collected by the IFU in a manner efficient enough to be completed within a week. Some preliminary findings resulting from our initial observations are presented, including a detailed spectral energy distribution analysis for one of our targets, the SMC's star cluster NGC 305. These findings are comparable to those obtained through other instruments. Additionally, we examine the properties of our spectral fits by comparing them to those obtained through other means, such as the masses of the cluster members and the properties of the cluster itself. Some exciting future research opportunities using ROSIE are also proposed. With its unique capabilities, we believe that ROSIE has the potential to significantly contribute to various fields of study, such as stellar populations, by allowing for the simultaneous analysis of numerous objects across a wide field of view. In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited, with an emphasis on updating existing knowledge of various aspects. Key topics covered include experimental methods used to achieve high energy particle collisions, the development of new and existing targets for these experiments, a review of recent C-C experiments, an overview of upcoming facilities, a discussion of the required purity of targets and beams, and the implementation of particle activation analysis to assess target contamination. Additionally, the paper considers future prospects for low-energy astrophysics research, such as the development of new radiative capture break-out energies and the study of the broad range of neutron-rich nuclei produced in astrophysical environments via the mechanism of the astrophysical S-factor. It is proposed that the sign and magnitude of the S-factor can serve as a chronometer for the timing and conditions of the initial stages of stellar development. Furthermore, the paper suggests exploring the potential of using the C-C break-out energy as an indicator of the core mass threshold in stellar compactness, a parameter that influences the stability of stellar evolution and structure. Some of the conclusions drawn from this research may be applicable to other nuclear reactions as well. Finally, the paper touches upon the broader implications of this research within the context of low-energy astrophysics. It highlights the significance of the first experiments, the role of the Helium-Helium fusion reaction in understanding the origin of Carbon, and the connection between the Carbon-Carbon break-out energy and the Core Mass Threshold in Stellar Development, which is marked by the onset of silent stellar collapse. Some of the concepts presented in this paper may also be relevant to other fields of study, such as Cosmology and Nuclear Physics. The process of devolatilisation in planetary bodies helps scientists comprehend the overall composition of terrestrial exoplanets. By applying this process in modelling, researchers can determine the approximate water and atmospheric gas content within these planets. Although the results indicate similar levels of water content among identical planets in diverse stellar environments, the remaining atmospheric components vary significantly, suggesting that further factors influence exoplanet composition beyond devolatilisation processes. To gain insight into the underlying physics, scientists must thoroughly examine the exoplanet system as a whole, incorporating both observational data and theoretical models. This new perspective is essential for accurately determining the essential properties of exoplanets. By studying the devolatilisation process and comparing theoretical models to real-world observations, scientists can dissect the complex interplay of physical mechanisms governing planetary development and evolution. This fresh approach can provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of planetary systems, enabling scientists to better understand the unique features of our Solar System and the extensive diversity of planetary systems discovered elsewhere. Ultimately, integrating devolatilisation models with diverse data sets will allow scientists to reconstruct the early history of planetary systems and the redshift evolution of the Universe. Deep neural networks have emerged as a promising solution for wireless localization based on channel state information, but relying solely on raw CSI proves ineffective due to its sensitivity to disturbances and ease of spoofing. To overcome these limitations, a novel CSI representation is developed through the incorporation of an autoencoder within a deep neural network framework, yielding an improved and resilient method known as DeepCSI. Unlike previous methods, DeepCSI can operate independently of channel models, enabling seamless integration with back-propagation and robust performance in the presence of adversarial attacks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, outperforming existing methods in indoor wireless localization scenarios. Furthermore, DeepCSI exhibits a high level of generalization across diverse environments, exhibiting a notable cross-site accuracy of 92%. This research offers a new paradigm for designing CSI representations, potentially expanding its applications to related tasks such as channel estimation. A comprehensive software framework is also provided to facilitate replication of these findings. This code can be accessed at https://github.com/ResearchAssist-ANL/DeepCSI. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework. Furthermore, this approach enables a unified treatment of diverse semantic structures, allowing them to be identified as equivalent through equivalence relations within the category. Moreover, this methodology allows for a systematic investigation of the relationship between the syntactical structure of the modal language and its associated semantic structures in the category. As a result, this method facilitates the identification of novel completeness results for cut-free sequent calculi for modal logics without additional decidability assumptions. Additionally, this approach also provides a general method for constructing maximal conservative extensions of modal logics and associated semantics. Finally, this method is further applied to study other logics such as intuitionistic negative admission and dynamic epistemic logic. Due to space constraints, the detailed applications of these methods to these logics are discussed in separate companion papers. For more information, see the separate supplementary document for modal logic, and another for the other considered logics. In particular, this research contributes a completeness result for a cut-free sequent calculus for the full positive intuitionistic negative admission logic without additional assumptions. In addition, this research provides a general method for constructing maximal conservative extensions of dynamic epistemic logic and proves the uniqueness of its standard extension using this method. In particular, this research shows that the standard extension of dynamic epistemic logic to modal logic is maximal and conservative, thus confirming existing results. In contrast, this research reveals that the standard extension of dynamic epistemic logic to conditional logic is not maximal and conservative when applied to the corresponding modal logic. We examine the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of Hamming graphs, demonstrating that many of the properties previously established for Grassmann graphs still apply to Hamming graphs. It's also shown that Hamming graphs attain optimal rank metric codes, and this result is further validated by analyzing closure properties and code lengths across various subgraphs derived from the Hamming graphs of optimal rank. Additionally, a metric characterisation of Hamming graphs of optimal rank is presented, along with a investigation of their embeddings within larger Hamming graphs. Furthermore, a method for iteratively constructing Hamming graphs of optimal rank is proposed, and this algorithm is also applied to generate such graphs for dimensions up to 6. Lastly, a connection between the eigenvalues of the Hamming graphs of optimal rank and the group actions of the Coxeter group is identified. To facilitate understanding, a detailed explanation of the irreducible characters of the Coxeter group is provided. Based on these results, a complete characterisation of the Hamming graphs of optimal rank in dimensions 3 and 4 is achieved, and this characterization is also extended to the graphs obtained from the partial Hamming graphs of optimal rank in dimensions 5. In the process, a code of maximal size relative to the rank and the partial Hamming graphs of optimal rank in dimension 6 is also determined. These findings are further substantiated by a computer code developed to verify the results. This code is also capable of generating the graphs of optimal rank in dimensions 7 and 8, and it has been made available for public use. To ensure the research's validity, a rigorous peer review process was applied to the work. Specifically, an initial version of the research was initially shared with experts in the field for comment, and then a comprehensive revision was undertaken in response to their feedback. The reliability of neural network-based inference depends on accurately assessing both inherent and outsourced uncertainties. We introduce a novel method for estimating inherent uncertainties associated with neural network-based regression, rooted in the connection between Gaussian processes and neural orchard plants. This method is combined with an existing approach for quantifying outsourced uncertainties, resulting in a comprehensive framework for proactive risk management. The capability of this framework is demonstrated through its application to simulated data, which compares favorably with traditional methods. Furthermore, the theoretical foundations of this framework are validated by an empirical analysis of inherent and outsourced uncertainties in the context of regression tasks. A supplementary code is available for reproduction of the results.

We prove that certain inclusions in quantum groups are quasi-split, which in turn implies the quasi-split nature of the associated non-commutative torus. The key to our proof is an equivalence between the category of quantum groups with inclusion and the category of non-commutative torus with map, accompanied by a functor that preserves this inclusion relationship. This equivalence holds for any inclusion of quantum groups that is regular and locally finite. When the underlying groups are simply connected, this inclusion is automatically quasi-split, which in turn allows us to generalize a previous result of Bishler and Müller to the realm of non-commutative torus. Furthermore, this generalization leads to a quasi-split characterization of non-commutative torus based on the commutativity of its classical limit. Additionally, we establish that any non-commutative torus can be decomposed into a product of quantum groups with commutative classical limits, each of which is locally finite and maximally dense. When the underlying groups are simply connected, this decomposition is unique and can be expressed in terms of the classical base space. Finally, we demonstrate that the quasi-split inclusions in quantum groups are precisely those that can be realized as the inclusion of functions on the group that are invariant under the action of a certain other group. Similarly, the quasi-split inclusions in non-commutative torus correspond to maps that preserve the inclusion relationship in the classical base space. These findings are encapsulated in a set of abstract theorems that can be applied to a wide range of specific situations. One such situation involves the inclusion of $SU_q(2)$ within $SL_q(3)$, which we prove to be quasi-split using a different method that is independent of our previous general results. This quasi-split inclusion in turn enables the construction of a non-commutative 2-torus with a classically commutative base space that cannot, however, be expressed as a product of quantum groups with commutative classical limits. Furthermore, we establish that any non-commutative torus can be expressed as a product of two such groups, with one being $SU_q(2)$ and the other an appropriately modified version of $SL_q(3)$. Policy iteration comes with computational limitations in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the cost of solving a large algebraic matrix equation in each iteration. In order to overcome these limitations, a method based on the Douglas-Rachford splitting has been developed and shows efficiency in a finite number of steps for evaluating policies in large-scale MDPs. This splitting was initially used for solving algebraic matrix equations in our previous work and we have now extended its application to policy iteration. We have also devised a variant of the splitting that is applicable to general monotone operators and is being used to accelerate policy iteration. The proposed methods are being evaluated through experiments on a variety of large-scale MDPs and outperform current best methods by a significant margin in value function approximation. For instance, a 20% improvement is observed in the computational time for evaluating policies in large-scale MDPs, with some tasks being solved 5 times faster than before. As a result, a substantial reduction in computational time is achieved, allowing us to evaluate policies on graphs with 100,000 nodes in less than 1 minute. Moreover, our method is found to be more effective than alternative techniques in reinforcement learning tasks involving graph-structured MDPs, resulting in a 15% improvement in task completion time. The proposed algorithms are being made available through an open-source repository on the Git Hub platform under the username 'franckd'. The repository contains a detailed explanation of the used methods and experimental settings, along with the code for reproducing the reported results. It is worth noting that our method is not proprietary and can be freely utilized by other researchers. Furthermore, the used techniques are applicable to a broader range of optimization problems in addition to policy iteration. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior. Additionally, the study presents formulas for calculating the Hankel determinants of edge ideals associated with weighted directed trees and oriented segment sets. These formulas are further applied to determine criteria for Hankel determinants to change sign with increasing rank in weighted directed trees and oriented segment sets. This study proposes a synthetic approach for generating numerous samples of rainfall and runoff data pairs using a computer simulation of hydrological models, which can then be applied to develop data-driven models, such as statistical and machine learning models, to improve their general performance and resilience to noise and irregularities in actual data sets. By creating large numbers of simulated data through probabilistic simulations, this method enables the creation of comprehensive virtual datasets that account for the inherent uncertainties in hydrological processes, thereby yielding better results than traditional methods. This paper investigates the feasibility of a robust learning paradigm where a certain percentage of labeled data can be trusted, while the remainder of the data is compromised by an adversary. In this robust learning framework, we focus on local data corruption, specifically the local membership query attack, in which the adversary can manipulate a percentage of examples by altering a specified percentage of their features. Our study reveals that even against this localized attack, all learnable parameters in common model architectures become unreadable once the attack's percentage exceeds a certain threshold, which is independent of the model's complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this localized attack has implications for the reliability of robustness certifications issued to neural network models, showing that these certifications are ineffective against the attack. To overcome this challenge, we propose a new robustness certification method that provides more accurate guarantees and is computationally feasible. Our certification method also enables the first sample-efficient algorithms for robust learning against localized attacks and achieves the best known performance in a related but less challenging problem. Our work also shows that these results apply to a broader range of related problems in attribute inference and counterfactual prediction. Last but not least, we conduct the first empirical analysis of localized attacks, revealing that they are prevalent in real-world datasets and that defenses against them are often inadequate.
