Hebbian theory offers a compelling framework for understanding how systems learn and represent information, especially in complex biological systems. A key advantage of Hebbian learning is its ability to facilitate learning processes that don't require external feedback. This can be achieved through a mechanism that causes simultaneously active neurons to have their connections strengthened. When viewed through the lens of system stability, this mechanism appears to be susceptible to causing oscillations or even instability. However, this apparent contradiction can be resolved by recognizing that Hebbian learning systems are, in fact, capable of converging onto stable states. In this study, we explore the mathematical underpinnings of Hebbian learning systems from a theoretical perspective, examining the conditions necessary for these systems to converge onto stable equilibria while ensuring the learning process remains stable and free from unnecessary oscillations. By adopting a general framework that is applicable across diverse system architectures, our research provides a unified understanding of Hebbian learning systems, revealing that these systems are inherently stable and capable of converging onto stable points when based on symmetric connection patterns. However, in cases where connection patterns are asymmetric, Hebbian learning systems may exhibit unstable dynamics, leading to oscillations or divergence. By recognizing the limitations of Hebbian learning systems, we identify potential avenues for improvement, paving the way for the development of more advanced learning algorithms based on Hebbian theory. Ultimately, this research is expected to contribute positively to the broader Hebbian research community while also opening doors for future innovations in the field. In addition to theoretical contributions, our research also offers a novel numerical method for analyzing and optimizing Hebbian learning systems based on differential equations, including the widely recognized Wilson-Cowan model. By applying this numerical method to the Wilson-Cowan model, we successfully demonstrated its applicability across diverse system architectures, confirming previous experimental findings and validating its effectiveness in analyzing complex dynamical systems. Furthermore, this numerical method enabled us to investigate the stability properties of Hebbian learning systems in a more nuanced and accurate manner, facilitating a deeper understanding of the Wilson-Cowan model and its potential applications in neuroscience and data analytics. By combining analytical and numerical approaches, our research provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing and optimizing Hebbian learning systems, including the Wilson-Cowan model, while also opening doors for future innovations in the field. In conclusion, this research contributes significantly to the Hebbian research community, offering novel theoretical and numerical insights that are expected to positively impact the broader scientific community while also paving the way for future advancements in the field. A new method has been introduced for generating entangled atomic states using a specialized interaction with a laser in a "hybrid atom interferometry" setting. Previous approaches have focused on using only magnetic or optical forces, but these methods have been hindered by efficiency losses due to technical noise. Our research reveals that entangled states can be created while keeping technical advancements separate from other advancements, thereby overcoming this limitation. We present a theoretical framework that outlines the conditions under which entangled states can be produced, and we provide concrete examples of its application in systems involving Rb and Cs atoms. Furthermore, we demonstrate through simulation that entangled states generated via this method can lead to enhanced resistance to technical noise in the entanglement metric. This means that entangled states may be more easily produced in practice, and our work has the potential to open up new avenues for the development of advanced atom interferometry systems. Additionally, our research may also be applied to other areas such as quantum simulation and protection. Lastly, our work is expected to contribute to the advancement of the precision of gravitation measurements in the future. \end{abstract} A new method has been introduced for generating entangled atomic states using a specialized interaction with a laser in a "hybrid atom interferometry" setting. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved impressive results across various languages and domains, but its high reliance on large amounts of labeled data makes it impractical in many scenarios. This paper proposes a self-supervised sequence annotation technique, integrated within a neural re-ranking framework, to alleviate this data requirement. By training the model to correct its own prediction errors, the self-supervised approach enables the transfer of valuable information from inaccurate outputs, ultimately enhancing the model's performance without relying on labeled data. When combined with limited supervised training, the self-supervised re-ranking method significantly boosts the model's performance on multiple languages and domains, outperforming traditional neural dependency parsing models trained solely on labeled data. Furthermore, the self-supervised model exhibits comparable performance to state-of-the-art unsupervised neural parsers on languages with extremely limited resources. The source code will be publicly available.

A specific query, known as CFI, which involves identifying a subset of vertices that contain a specific number of frontier vertices, is examined in detail. The study reveals that the CFI query is not generally expressible within the Eaton-Bullcock framework but shows that it can be effectively formulated using CPT for specific, isolated graph classes. Conversely, it is demonstrated that the CFI query is definable within the CPT framework for any class of graphs that includes only isolated graphs but is indefinable if it contains a single infinite graph structure. Additionally, the research identifies necessary and sufficient conditions for classes of graphs to be able to handle CFI-queries that involve any integer value, which is a previously unsolved problem. The study also examines relationships between CFI and other queries, revealing that it is more complex than the CFQi queries for i greater than or equal to 2, yet less complex than the CQ∃R and CFM queries. A new lower bound is established for CPT in terms of these other query types, while further research opens up new avenues for investigation. All key results were formally proven and all tests were conducted within the SygusT framework. A new tool, called Cefeb, was also developed to verify the results and check the bounds. Cefeb is based on the SygusT framework and uses a novel approach to generate and verify CPT instances that match the CFI queries of interest. Cefeb was used to verify all the key results and test various query types, including CFI, CFM and CQ∃R, for which the generated CPT expressions match the expected patterns. Cefeb is composed of approximately 500 lines of code and is available on github at the address https://github.com/alexanderbuchanan/CEFEb. CEFeb is a new tool in the field of formal verification that is based on the SygusT framework and is used to check the complexity of first-order logic queries on classes of graph structures. CEFeb was developed by Alexander Buchanan in collaboration with Luke Siewert and is now available for public use. CEFeb is capable of formally verifying the complexity of various first-order logic queries on classes of graph structures within a finite amount of time. In the compound Eu2Ir2O7, a type-II Weyl semimetal exhibits $A$-type antiferromagnetic order with a unique transition to long-range order upon doping, where the initial insulating phase transitions to a metal with a unique order. We have investigated the effects of doping Eu2Ir2O7 with Bi at the Eu site, using neutron scattering to analyze the changes in its magnetic and lattice structures. As a result of Bi doping, the $A$-type antiferromagnetic order decreases in proportion to the dopant concentration and so does the transition temperature, while the structure undergoes noticeable changes with significant increases in the lattice volume and the thermal vibration of atoms. These observations indicate that Bi4$^{3+}$ preferentially occupies the Eu site and that the long-range order of the material is easily disrupted by small concentrations of dopants at the Eu site. Furthermore, our research reveals that the valence state of Ir in the material remains unchanged across the entire doping range, with the compound transitioning from an insulator to a metal due to the disruption of its magnetic order by Bi doping rather than any change in its electronic configuration. Our research provides the first evidence of a direct transition between an antiferromagnetic Weyl semimetal and a paramagnetic metal, paving the way for further studies on the properties and behavior of this material type. Additionally, our research demonstrates that neutron scattering can effectively analyze the effects of doping on materials even when they are paramagnetic, provided that the dopant has a significantly larger neutron absorption cross-section than the constituent atoms of the material. This highlights the significance of using neutron scattering as a powerful diagnostic tool for investigating the properties of materials. Based on our research findings, we propose that the material with optimal Bi doping at 10.6% Bi doping, Bi2.6Eu0.6Ir2O7, exhibits a unique characteristic of being a paramagnetic metal with a unique combination of lattice structure, magnetic order, and electronic properties, distinct from any previously known materials. This research opens up new avenues for further studies on the properties and behavior of this novel material type. Additionally, our research demonstrates that the material with optimal Bi doping at 10.6% Bi doping, Bi2.6Eu0.6Ir2O7, exhibits a unique combination of lattice structure, magnetic order, and electronic properties, distinct from any previously known materials. This research opens up new avenues for further studies on the properties and behavior of this novel material type.

The purpose of this research is to investigate specific groups of random variables, known as cyclic n-tuples, where each variable has a unique set of values that add up to a non-zero, constant value 'r'. This constant 'r' is divisible by n, which represents a positive integer greater than one. Initially, we will establish general principles for simulating cyclic n-tuples in both uniform and random distributions. Next, we will explore specific methods for generating such distributions, starting with a basic approach using an inverse cumulative distribution function method, followed by alternative methods such as the rejection algorithm and others. We will also examine how these general principles can be adapted to generate cyclic n-tuples with specific characteristics in various fields such as finance and Markov processes. Ultimately, we will validate the efficacy of these methods through empirical analysis. Interestingly, one of the key outcomes of this research is the discovery that one of these methods can outperform others in a specific scenario, which may hold broader implications for the field of probabilistic modeling. As a result, we hope that these results will motivate further research in this area. Moreover, the findings of this study may also be applicable in other fields where cyclic n-tuples could be useful. For instance, they could potentially be applied in the analysis of dependent continuous random variables or in the modeling of financial concepts such as contingent payment structures or Markovian payment systems. It is also worth noting that one of the key contributions of this research is the establishment of a clear distinction between true dependencies and apparent dependencies resulting from non-trivial correlations, which may be particularly significant in fields such as medicine and social sciences. Finally, we will demonstrate the practical utility of the theorems and algorithms presented in this study through two real-world case studies. The first case involves modeling the payment structure of a life insurance policy, while the second involves modeling the payment structure of a loan. In both instances, we successfully employed our proposed methods to generate cyclic n-tuples in order to calculate the present value of future payments. The outcomes of these applications confirm the exceptional accuracy and efficiency of the proposed methods. The source code underlying these applications is freely available for public use on the repository https://github.com/AdityaBhatnagar/ProbabilisticMarkovProcesses. Similarly, the results presented in this research are reproducible through the document https://adityabhatnagar.github.io/ProbabilisticMarkovProcesses/. Many software systems are designed to be adaptable through run-time settings, but this configuration often goes unused or varies minimably among deployments, also resulting in unchanged non-functional properties. This scenario presents an opportunity for optimization: can we reduce a system's variability in configurations that affect performance or other important aspects? To investigate this question, we developed a method to identify and analyze relevant configuration dimensions in open-source applications. The method was applied to 12 widely-used Python projects, revealing a significant number of potential configuration options (on average, 214 dimensions across the projects). However, our results show that the majority of these dimensions have minimal impact on a system's behavior or would be difficult to adjust at run-time. Conversely, configurations associated with performance or other important properties are often associated with low complexity. This finding suggests that selectively optimizing run-time configurations can be beneficial, potentially leading to performance gains without compromising binary size or other critical metrics. To facilitate further research, we have made our analysis available online, including the configuration spaces of the projects we studied. This resource can be accessed through our repository at https://github.com/complex-systems-lab/config-var-survey. Light dark matter particles, particularly those weighing less than a GeV, are considered standard model extensions, whereas particles with weights of several GeV are considered as possible options. Directly detecting such lightweight sub-GeV dark matter is challenging due to weak nuclear interactions. Even if detected, the signal would likely be ambiguous and difficult to confirm. Building on previous research, we examined the potential for confirming sub-GeV dark matter candidates with weights between 40 MeV and 1 GeV. Our analysis reveals that weighing around 200 million germanium target atoms over five years could help rule out or confirm a wide range of cross-section values for dark matter candidates within this weight range. Furthermore, we found that the required measurement precision for germanium nuclear recoil events is within the same order as detecting individual alpha decays. Moreover, we discovered that the same experiment could also discover additional physics such as the Langan-Cabibbo suppressed decay of the $b \rightarrow s$ transition or even the existence of extra $Z'$ bosons with masses below 20 GeV. Ultimately, successfully confirming sub-GeV dark matter would mark a groundbreaking achievement in the history of particle physics experimentation. Additionally, achieving this breakthrough might also open doors to discovering novel physics in the $b \rightarrow s$ transition or dark photon searches in the same experiment. This research introduces a novel anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction model to create entangled states, presenting two distinct methods in the process. The first approach leverages Rabi oscillations by comparing the probabilities of two entangled states, $\ket{\psi_{\pm}} = \ket{2}_{\mathrm{q}} \otimes \ket{\pm 2}_{\mathrm{f}}$. The second method employs the states' differences to form an entangled light-matter qubit, focusing on the symmetric state $\ket{\psi_{+}}$. Both methods are applicable in both the strong and weak coupling regimes, with simulations using a trimer microwave cavity confirmed the efficacy of this anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction model. Furthermore, this study explores the impact of environment influence using a Markov method to model dissipation. The findings indicate that high entropic measures can coexist with minimal effects on Rabi-like oscillations, suggesting opportunities for applying this concept in experimental settings. Measuring heart rate variability (HRV) from the interbeat interval flags potential cardiovascular risks and predicts adverse outcomes, making it a vital tool for health monitoring and predicting mortality risk (HRV). Accurate HRV measurement is hindered by artifacts in interbeat interval data, typically filtered using sophisticated and computationally expensive techniques. Researchers have found that a simpler approach, incorporating a Markov process, effectively estimates HRV from noisy data, outperforming existing methods. This approach is further combined with an evolutionary algorithm to create a method that can learn and estimate HRV from raw signal data without prior knowledge. Experimental results confirm that this approach can accurately estimate HRV while reducing computational costs. Additionally, HRV is used to predict mortality risk in patients with congestive heart failure (CHF), and the Markov-based method is found to improve the accuracy of these predictions. Finally, the HRV model is used to estimate the mortality risk of patients with essential hypertension, and the evolutionarily optimized Markov model is found to outperform other methods in this application. This research presents novel and efficient methods for estimating HRV that can be applied to various clinical tasks. Furthermore, these methods are implemented in open-source software that can be easily integrated into existing clinical tools for automated HRV analysis. This approach has the potential to improve the diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular diseases. Ultimately, the HRV-based model shows promise in predicting mortality risk in patients with essential hypertension. This research suggests that HRV, a simple and cost-effective indicator of cardiovascular health, can be effectively used to identify at-risk patients. This approach can be applied to various clinical tasks involving the estimation of physiological parameters. We analyze large deviations of the power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confining potential. The particle is driven by a steady stream of active forces modeled as independent, independent and identically distributed in both time and position. The system is governed by the solution to a generalized McKean-Vlasov equation. The rate function that measures the likelihood of observing specific power inputs in comparison to its average value is determined through an optimization problem. The results show that the rate function is consistently optimal across both free and confining scenarios, and its form can be fully characterized. Moreover, the case without the confining potential aligns with previous research findings. The theory is further validated by numerical simulations that match the calculated large deviations with the observed fluctuations in power inputs within the confining scenario. The research provides a framework for analyzing the dynamics of active particles subjected to various types of potentials. The methodology employed is expected to be applicable to the broader class of stochastic dynamics models that include both active and passive forces. The model of the AOUP, however, specifically excludes certain types of forces that are known to cause instabilities, as they are modeled as a sum of independent forces in both time and space. The research is further expanded to discuss its implications in relation to the second law of thermodynamics. The discussion highlights the challenges associated with extending the principle of increasing entropy beyond systems that include living organisms. The research concludes by noting the potential applications of the theory in analyzing the thermodynamics of microscopic machines. The research is primarily theoretical in nature and relies on analytical solutions to optimize a particular problem. The results are verified through numerical simulations conducted using Python code. The code is included as part of the research in the form of comments and explanations. The research is expected to contribute to the broader field of stochastic dynamics, and specifically, to the analysis of active particles. The primary contribution is the derivation of a general method for calculating the rate function for power inputs within any confining potential. The research is further expected to contribute to the ongoing discussion regarding the second law of thermodynamics and its implications for living organisms. This paper introduces HUMBI, a large, high-resolution dataset of human body expressions in 3D that focuses on modeling everyday gestures and emotions. Composed of multi-person footage with five major signals - head, hand, hip, spine, and face - HUMBI is distinct from existing human body expression datasets, which typically feature single signals. HUMBI facilitates efficient training and testing of multi-person 3D human expression models. Notably, HUMBI differs from other datasets through its inclusion of complex hip and spine signals, which are crucial for capturing subtle emotional and gestural displays. Captured using high-resolution cameras, HUMBI contains rich and detailed footage beneficial for advanced learning techniques. HUMBI is prepared for release, along with a proposed method for creating more realistic and engaging hip and spine animations. Experimental results demonstrate that HUMBI significantly enhances the performance of existing models in 3D human expression tasks. Specifically, HUMBI achieves notable gains of 5.0% and 3.1% in accuracy on the Human3.6M and HUMBI-datasets, respectively. Ultimately, HUMBI has the potential to inspire novel research in modeling human body expressions and can be used to create more authentic and captivating virtual characters. Additionally, HUMBI may be applied in developing advanced human-like robots. HUMBI is accessible at https://humbi Dataset.github.io/. A supplementary video is available at https://youtu.be/6Q8Q8Q8Q8Q.be.

While multilingual neural language models have achieved great success in translating between different languages, they often require a substantial amount of work to adapt models from one language to another. We developed a general framework that can efficiently transfer neural models from English to other languages, simply by modifying the model's input. In our framework, we utilize the existing translation of an out-of-vocabulary word in the target language, rather than waiting for a new model to be trained. We evaluated our approach on six language pairs and discovered that it yields significant improvements over the current state-of-the-art methods, often with minimal additional resources required. We also observed that this transfer is highly effective even for languages that are very different from English, such as Japanese and Korean. Notably, our results show that this transfer is highly effective for Korean, outperforming a model trained from scratch on a large-scale corpus. We hope that our framework will facilitate the development of multilingual neural models for lesser-resourced languages. More details can be found on our project page at https://nlp.stanford.edu/~mnarayan/translating-language-models/. The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/narayanm/translate-nlm. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single dynamics model for multiple tasks may lead to subpar results compared
to training separate models for individual tasks. However, we did discover
a novel method where multiple tasks are trained simultaneously to extract a
global representation from state and action data, resulting in significant
performance enhancements compared to models that extract information from either
states or actions in isolation. We further demonstrate that this shared
representation can be transferred to improve performance on new tasks introduced
after initial training. Additionally, our method outperformed existing model-based
multi-task reinforcement learning approaches in empirical tests across grid-world
and MuJoCo robotic simulations. We refer to our technique as Multi-Task State-
Action Embeddings (MT-SAE). By applying a similar concept to existing multi-task
reinforcement learning techniques, we observed substantial performance boosts in
complex robotic simulation tasks. Our code is available online for public access.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. A specialized algorithm is developed to quickly determine the affected substations and calculate the resulting load reduction and distribution feeder damage resulting from storm surge and wind power outages. Utilizing storm surge water levels and hurricane wind speeds, the study generates probabilistic scenarios of system configurations, which are used to develop a probabilistic model of the power system. This model enables rapid assessment of system impacts during combined hurricane and storm surge events. Specifically, the study demonstrates the proposed model's capabilities in analyzing the effects of such events on a substantial power grid representing northeastern US cities. The study shows that the proposed model can efficiently handle large systems, performing computations within minutes that would typically take hours using other methods. Some notable findings from applying the model include the identification of power substations likely to experience storm surge-related outages, estimation of total system load reduction, calculation of total feeder damage, and prioritization of substations for restoration following a hurricane, which is particularly important for enhancing post-hurricane power restoration efficiency. Some of these findings indicate that storm surge damage far exceeds that caused by hurricane wind, and that key transmission lines and major power substations are at high risk of experiencing storm surge-related outages. Some of the load-reduced substations are found to have spare capacity despite being disconnected from the main grid, which could be utilized to supply other load-reduced substations during combined hurricane and storm surge events. Some of the main transmission lines are found to experience multiple outages due to storm surge situations, which could lead to significant power losses and hinder grid restoration after a hurricane. Some of the power substations in coastal areas are found to experience outages more frequently than those in other areas, which could be attributed to higher storm surge water levels in these regions. Some of the power substations in low-lying areas are found to experience outages more frequently than those in other areas, which could be attributed to higher storm surge water levels in these regions. Some of the key transmission lines are found to experience outages more frequently than others, which could be attributed to storm surge water levels reaching as high as 12 feet in some areas. We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D spaces, which exhibit unpredictable behavior in their trajectories, analogous to the classic H\'enon map but with an added benefit of simplifiable coordinate representations. This uniqueness of these generalized heterochaos baker maps lies in their ability to model dynamic systems with complex dynamics while maintaining easily checkable conditions for their local coordinate changes, which is particularly useful for analyzing heavy periodic orbits. We developed pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks where the dilation factor varies according to the pitch, effectively spanning a wide range of temporal scales within a single network framework. We compared our method with existing waveform synthesis techniques, including vector quantized VAE and its variants, as well as supersample-scramble approach, in terms of reconstruction quality and sample diversity. We observed that our approach yields more varied samples when compared to the supersample-scramble method, achieves better reconstruction quality than the VQGAN and its variants on Mel Cepstral coefficients, and enables more efficient encoding of shorter audio segments while maintaining similar reconstruction quality and sample diversity. Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant approach, struggle with ensuring user data privacy. This study delves into the core challenges of CF, identifying data sparsity and cold starting issues. To address these problems, a new Privacy-Aware Hybrid Recommender System is introduced, combining CF with a natural text-based method. This innovative system not only mitigates data sparsity and cold starting issues but also protects user data from unauthorized access. Leveraging the Focused Gaussian Mechanism framework, it efficiently maintains privacy while minimizing performance degradation. The proposed method is evaluated using real-world datasets, outperforming traditional CF-based methods across multiple metrics in terms of accuracy and recommendation quality. Furthermore, experiments demonstrate that the implemented algorithms scale well in terms of computational complexity. Therefore, this study provides a viable solution for designing and deploying recommender systems that prioritize user data privacy and address key challenges. This approach is poised to contribute to the development of more effective and privacy-respecting recommender systems in the future. The detection of exoplanets using the Doppler method is significantly hampered by stellar activity, which creates false positive signals. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed new indicators to measure stellar activity levels, such as using the He I 6788 angstroms spectral line. This study examines the He I 6788 angstroms line as an indicator of stellar activity in G-K type main sequence stars. It involves analyzing data from 43 stars with known activity levels, and finds that this line is affected by both activity and temperature fluctuations. Furthermore, the study discovers that activity-related changes in the line are more pronounced in faster-rotating stars. Ultimately, the He I 6788 angstroms line shows promise as a useful tool for distinguishing between planet-induced Doppler signals and those caused by stellar activity. Additionally, the study provides constraints on He I 6788 angstroms line behavior under inactive conditions, which can aid in modeling this line in active stars. Finally, the study suggests that the He I 6788 angstroms line may be a suitable substitute for the Ca II H&K lines in certain applications. Overall, the research offers insights into the He I 6788 angstroms line behavior, and highlights its potential as a valuable tool for understanding stellar activity and detecting exoplanets. To further explore these findings, the study includes a new code, HEI2DOP, which models the He I 6788 angstroms line as a function of both activity and temperature fluctuations. This code can be utilized to remove activity-related effects from the line, and ultimately improve the detection of exoplanets using the Doppler method. By combining the HEI2DOP code with data from stellar spectra, researchers can accurately remove activity-related variability and recover Doppler signals from active stars. As a proof of concept, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of the HEI2DOP code in recovering exoplanet signals from the M dwarf star, Proximae Centauri. By employing the code, researchers were able to detect the planet signals that had been previously obscured by stellar activity. To investigate zero-energy peaks in tunneling conductance, we developed a theoretical framework for varying tunneling strength and temperature. The model reveals distinct peaks at zero energy, arising from different physical phenomena, which exhibit contrasting responses to temperature and tunneling strength variations. Conductance spectra, obtained via numerical simulation, show a non-monotonic relationship with tunneling strength. As temperature is decreased, the width of the peak diminishes, whereas an increase in tunneling strength initially narrows the peak but eventually broadens it at zero energy, a phenomenon also observed in other non-localized states. Moreover, we derived explicit equations for conductance, applying models of localized and non-localized zero-energy states, and compared these with numerical simulations. The developed framework is versatile and can be applied to different systems, such as those with Majorana modes, competition between localized and non-localized states at zero energy, and topological superconducting surfaces with fermion parity's spontaneous breaking. Furthermore, we explored the application of second harmonic generation in tunneling experiments to distinguish between different physical phenomena producing zero-energy peaks. The results of our study have significant implications for the interpretation of tunneling conductance measurements, particularly in experiments on topological superconducting surfaces, where the observed zero-energy peaks are often attributed to Majorana modes. However, our findings indicate that the peak can arise from other physical phenomena as well, including spontaneous breaking of fermion parity in the presence of a competition between localized and non-localized states at zero energy. Consequently, we suggest alternative methods for confirming the presence of Majorana modes, such as utilizing second harmonic generation in tunneling experiments to produce distinct signatures for different physical phenomena. The proposed approach enables a thorough examination of the origin of zero-energy peaks in tunneling conductance measurements, thereby enhancing the reliability of experimental findings. Additionally, we outline potential future research directions, including the investigation of zero-energy peaks in systems of interacting fermions and the exploration of non-equilibrium transport phenomena. Furthermore, we highlight the potential for tunneling experiments to distinguish between different topological orders in a single system, a capability that could be leveraged to develop topological quantum computers. The study concludes by highlighting the significant scientific challenges associated with realizing such a prototype, including the need for advances in quantum measurement techniques and the development of more sophisticated algorithms for extracting topological properties from tunneling conductance data. Nevertheless, we emphasize the potential for tunneling experiments to play a pivotal role in achieving a major breakthrough in this field, thereby opening up new avenues for quantum computing technology

Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of Morita invariance for shadows, one that is both more accessible and less reliant on references compared to existing proofs. Additionally, the relationship between shadows and THH is utilized to derive axiomatic characterizations of stable homotopy theories (as formulated by Berman) and, more generally, the characterizations apply to functors with extensions to stable homotopy classes of cocycles. Finally, it is shown that shadows provide an innovative approach to computing THH of certain bicategories, such as the category of simplicial sets, by utilizing a cocycle construction that parallels the development of THH. Consequently, this result provides a direct proof that shadows are equivalent to THH on the category of simplicial sets. Current approaches to image editing tasks, such as color grading, typically apply pre-defined transformations to entire images. However, operations like this often have ambiguous outcomes and require customization. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel method that enables personalized single-image color grading without needing paired examples. Our approach relies on an underdetermined linear regression problem that allows for a multitude of solutions. To overcome this uncertainty, it utilizes input-output similarity relationships in a unified framework. This technique delivers superior performance in comparison to state-of-the-art methods across various real-world applications, including color grading, degrading, and sketch-based image editing. Additionally, it achieves impressive results in unsupervised intrinsic image decomposition, outperforming existing methods. Due to its efficiency, it can process images in real-time. This technique is now available as a browser extension called ColGrad. colgrad.org.uk

The exponential growth in data volume over short periods of time poses significant challenges for real-time applications across fields like high energy physics, cosmology, and machine learning system testing. This surge necessitates the immediate processing and analysis of data at the source to extract actionable insights within a condensed timeframe. To meet this demand, Infiniband has emerged as a leading data transfer technology, offering high bandwidth and low latency data transfer capabilities essential for real-time data analysis. However, the variability in real-world data transfer scenarios makes it crucial to accurately predict bandwidth requirements to prevent data transfer congestion. This paper introduces a novel, real-time and scalable algorithm called BDIAn (Bandwidth Distribution Identification Algorithm) to dynamically detect the distribution of bandwidth at the Infiniband fabric during real-time data transfers. BDIAn employs a sophisticated, parameter-free data structure called the B-DI tree to identify bandwidth distribution patterns, utilizing a combination of hash tables and link lists for optimal performance. The algorithm has undergone extensive testing on various Infiniband cluster interconnects, demonstrating its capacity to detect bandwidth distribution patterns within milliseconds with a high degree of accuracy. The results show BDIAn outperforms existing solutions by delivering faster and more precise bandwidth distribution identification compared to Anon and VMAP. Furthermore, a comparative analysis with SmartNIC-based approaches reveals BDIAn offers a more efficient solution, requiring minimal host CPU resources and no reliance on additional hardware. In this study, researchers explore a specific type of problem associated with cghs: saturation problems that correspond to earlier studied extremal issues. Using a mathematical model that represents a linear programming relaxation of the saturation problem, researchers investigate the value of the optimal solution and demonstrate that this value remains unchanged at a specific constant for certain geometric hypergraphs. Additionally, by constructing specific examples, saturation problems are shown to be NP-hard in both the general case of cghs and for two specific subcategories, thereby highlighting a computational complexity aspect. Lastly, some specific upper bounds on the maximum size of saturated subsets within certain types of geometric hypergraphs are established. These findings contribute to a broader understanding of geometric hypergraphs and their associated saturation problems. A novel robotic approach inspired by the lamprey's ability to climb smooth surfaces has been developed. The resulting robot, Trident, features a unique trailing tail that facilitates a smooth, continuous climbing motion while generating substantial vertical movement. Through experimentation, it was demonstrated that the optimal vertical stride displacement ranges from 60% to 80% of the height being overcome. The robot's peak vertical stride distance of 85% was attributed to the occurrence of a trailing tail flip. Furthermore, the optimal horizontal stride distance was found to be greater than the height being overcome. Numerical models were also created to analyze the relationship between robot design parameters and performance, ultimately guiding the design of an improved version with enhanced climbing capabilities. The new design was shown to be capable of reaching a peak vertical stride distance of 90% and to be highly resilient to variations in body length and width. The developed robots were successfully tested in a series of in vivo and in vitro experiments, showcasing their ability to climb various heights both inside animals and on a smooth surface. The research was found to have significant implications for both robotics and neuroscience applications. The newly designed robots were also found to be highly effective at delivering therapeutic medication deep into the bodies of small animals. This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of cancer-induced mortality through a probabilistic modeling approach. By solving the Fokker-Planck equation, this method generates detailed information about the tumor's probabilistic dynamics. There are two key novelty aspects to this framework: Firstly, it employs a probabilistic modeling approach to tackle the difficult problem of multi-objective optimization in cancer treatment; Secondly, it leverages Monte Carlo simulations and uncertainty quantification techniques to generate comprehensive statistics, such as mean and standard deviation, which enable the comparison of various treatment strategies. The proposed framework is applied to a model of endocrine therapy with two treatment approaches, uncovering the optimal combination of doses that maximizes the probability of prolonged remission or cure while simultaneously increasing the likelihood of a good quality of life. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this framework, revealing a range of statistically reliable outcomes for various levels of resource investment. Furthermore, the underlying methodology is adaptable to a broad class of dynamical systems, making it highly versatile. Finally, suggestions are provided for applying this framework to other complex optimization challenges in biomedical research. This study examines the short-term and long-term resource allocation problems in device-to-device (D2D) communication networks, focusing on minimizing the overall network latency. In the short-term context, we aim to achieve the lowest end-to-end delay by optimizing message transmission times. Conversely, the long-term perspective involves addressing delay disparities. To resolve this issue, we employ a weighted fair scheduling approach, aiming to balance fairness and overall network latency. Key performance indicators, such as throughput, interference, and delay, are also thoroughly considered. Simulation results validate the efficacy of the proposed algorithms in attaining optimal short-term latency and ensuring fair resource allocation in the long-term scenario. Notably, the long-term algorithm exhibits near-optimal performance while exhibiting a linear computational complexity. Overall, our algorithms strike a balance between fairness and system latency. Furthermore, we propose an initial algorithm for dynamically adjusting D2D link establishment and amplify-and-forward relay usage in mixed D2D and cellular networks, focusing on minimizing the total end-to-end delay. Notably, the efficacy of the proposed methods is evaluated under both ideal and imperfect channel knowledge conditions. Event identification is a crucial task on dynamic graphs as nodes evolve over time, enabling the detection of associations and disassociations. However, node representation faces difficulties due to nodes disappearing, emerging, or changing their characteristics, making it challenging to obtain stable and meaningful event-related nodes. To address this issue, we propose a method called DyGraphformer that utilizes a transformer-based architecture in a hierarchical manner. It excels at node embedding by focusing on adjacent time steps and subgraphs, while also capturing long-term global patterns. Additionally, we employ an encoder-decoder structure along with a graph transformer to capture the dynamic patterns of nodes and their interactions. Experimental results on widely used datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we provide step-by-step guidance for reproducing our results to facilitate further research. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/juansalas/DyGraphformer.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show how these theoretical solutions can be accurately reproduced in Lagrangian hydrodynamic simulations, thereby validating and verifying these codes for a range of scenarios. This study's findings are expected to be useful for assessing the reliability of shock-accurate compressive and radiative hydrodynamics codes on high-speed, self-similar shock waves. Most importantly, we explore the connection between the similarity properties of the initial density distribution and the similarity behavior of the pressure and temperature behind the shock wave. Notably, when the density distribution is a power law, the pressure and temperature behind the shock also exhibit similar power law behaviors, identical to the density exponent. This unexpected relationship holds true for all values of the adiabatic index and spatial density exponents, suggesting a universal thermodynamic similarity for strongly accelerating shock waves in an ideal gas. Finally, we discuss the potential implications of this universal thermodynamic similarity for non-ideal gases, while also highlighting the unique characteristics of the most intensely accelerating shock waves, particularly those with high values of the density exponent and low values of the adiabatic index. In such extreme cases, the thermodynamic similarity behind the shock gives way to a different type of similarity behavior, characterized by a sharp decrease in pressure and temperature as the shock intensity increases. This unusual phenomenon is found to occur gradually for certain gas types and parameter settings, but can potentially change abruptly through complex dynamics. Nonetheless, for the ideal gas case, the thermodynamic similarity behind the shock remains unchanged, even at very high values of the density exponent and low values of the adiabatic index. This unusual behavior highlights the intricate and complex nature of accelerating shock waves in an ideal gas. This novel plasma generation method is found to be highly efficient, as it enables the attainment of extremely low final pressures with minimal required laser energy, an improvement over conventional techniques. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive cancers. The process of histopathological characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia. Manual examination of these samples by skilled pathologists is necessary, but the method's effectiveness is limited by its labor-intensive and time-consuming nature. The problem is exacerbated by the increasing global burden of colorectal cancer. To address this, researchers have been developing computer-assisted diagnosis systems to aid in quick and accurate characterization of colorectal polyps. These systems typically rely on deep learning architectures, but their performance is often hampered by the requirement for large, balanced datasets. The case is different for medical imaging tasks, where finding suitable training data can be challenging and expensive to scale. In response, a novel method has been proposed that utilizes a combination of maximum likelihood estimation and information theory to improve classification performance in the absence of sufficient data. The approach has been tested on a comprehensive dataset of 11499 images and has demonstrated superior performance, with an average AUC of 0.933 across three diverse benchmarks. The results indicate that the proposed technique can achieve high accuracy in characterizing colorectal polyps even when datasets are limited. This study examines the most severe data loss when using a universal source encoder that is chosen by an adversary, leading to the most critical classification of an encoded message. By solving this problem in various settings, we derive upper limits on the most stringent data loss rate, which can be seen as a maximally secure source code. Specifically, in the scenario where an adversary perfectly guesses the source, our results confirm a long-standing open question by showing the existence of a universal encoder that allows an adversary to guess the source with an accuracy of at most $2^{-n/H(X)}$, where $H(X)$ represents the source's entropy, $n$ is the codeword length, and this bound is within a constant factor of the best previously known limit. Furthermore, we investigate how this problem changes when there are multiple encoding methods available to the transmitter and how it is affected when an internal part of the transmitter, rather than an external adversary, chooses the encoder. Additionally, we explore connections to the study of randomness bounds in coding theory. Our study also leads to new bounds on the secure transmission of continuous sources, including a generalization of the Shannon grid, which is the most secure method for transmitting continuous sources with an additive distortion measure. Deep learning-trained generative models can function as a framework for imaging from limited measurements, such as sparse data sets, by deconvolving a latent space representation. In our study, we utilize and adapt this concept to multiview video capture, achieving a breakthrough in recovering multiple video inputs from a single compressed sequence. Our novel framework, CompressGAN, employs a compressed video input combined with an associated metadata representation to generate high-quality, synchronized multiview video content. By iterating between model training and compressed inference, CompressGAN outperformed existing methods in producing high-fidelity, real-world multiview video data and achieved superior performance in compressed video inference and cross-view video translation tasks. Notably, our generated content was preferred over real data in these tasks, indicating its high quality. Additionally, our platform enabled the creation of extensive multiview video datasets captured with synthetic sensors, paving the way for research in this field. Our source code and generated content are publicly available for download at the provided link.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs an alternating sequence of quantum and classical operations to optimize a classical binary objective function, defined by spins represented by qubits. The optimal solution is typically achieved by adjusting the amplitude and phase parameters of the quantum operations through a classical optimization process, with the quality of the outcome depending on these parameters. However, the QAOA performance is limited by the constraints of quantum hardware, so a local classical optimization method is applied within a global quantum one to refine the results. The researchers combined this approach with another technique, the classical descent method, to improve the local refinement. The hybridized strategy led to significant enhancements in the outcomes compared to using the original local refinement or the descent method independently. The enhanced QAOA was successfully tested on a challenging problem, specifically the Max-Cut on a double triangle graph with two cliques of equal size, under various parameter settings. The experiments showed substantial improvement in the objective function value, amounting to an increase of around 50 percent over the standard QAOA approach under similar conditions. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial for various clinical applications, but common disorders and diseases often obstruct their accurate detection due to significant structural modifications. For example, vertebrae osteomyelitis causes bone density alterations, while vertebral compression fractures leads to abnormal shape and size changes. To address these challenges, a novel and robust multi-path vertebrae identification network is proposed to simultaneously detect multiple vertebrae with an end-to-end approach, regardless of their positions. By integrating multiple prediction paths, the network integrates contextual and detailed information to improve overall performance and resilience to vertebrae appearance variations. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed model over existing state-of-the-art models on two public spinal CT scan datasets. Furthermore, ablation experiments confirm the synergistic benefits of the multi-path structure over single-path models.
